speechtext:
Mr. GUTHRIE moved that Bill (No. 220) to incorporate the Albert and Moncton Railway Company be placed on the orders of this day, immediately after routine proceedings, for consideration in Committee of the Whole, in accordance with the recommendation contained in the twenty-second report of the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.
* Mr. SPROULE. I think there is too much of this kind of procedure of late. It gives very little time for consideration; the Bill will no doubt be taken up at once. 'Then we are not by any means at the end of the session, but only going to adjourn for a while. The Bill cannot be delayed 'long, and I think it should stand over 'until after the adjournment.

maintopic: THE ALBERT AND MONCTON RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The Bill for the Albert railway was adopted by the committee without any amendment, and this seems to be the only opportunity offered to pass the Bill. There is no controversy about it. I do not see any reason why we should not get rid of that Bill.

maintopic: THE ALBERT AND MONCTON RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: While agreeing with the general remarks of my hon. friend from Grey (Mr., Sproule), I want to say with respect to this Bill that unless it is passed now it will very materially delay the development of the shale interests in Albert county. They have for many years lain dormant, but there is every prospect now that, if facilities are not afforded, the English capitalists who are on the spot, and have been on the spot, may be delayed in developing that property. The railway runs from Hillsboro, where large plaster quarries are situated, out into the Baltimore district where the shale quarries are found. The distance to Moncton is about twenty miles. It is for industrial development, and simply because we are going to have a recess is no reason why, if it is at all possible, to have this Bill passed, it should be delayed. We want to go into this business at once, and why should the Bill be delayed until September?

maintopic: THE ALBERT AND MONCTON RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman state why the Bill was so late in coming before the House?

maintopic: THE ALBERT AND MONCTON RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
It came from the Senate. The parties from England only came over late during the session, arrange-

ments were only completed very recently, and I think they have moved in the matter with great expedition. It has only been possible to reach this Bill from the Senate within a 'day or two, and I felt it my duty, in the interests of that section of the country, to attempt to expedite the Bill. I do not see that any interests will suffer; the Bill is not contentious. It is a standard Bill and passed through the Railway Committee unanimously.
1 Mr. SPROULE. We do not touch private Bills to-day, this being Thursday, and we will reach private Bills to-morrow, when it is very likely to pass. Therefore, there is no urgency from that standpoint. If it passed the committee without any amendment. there is not likely to be any delay in the House. Let it take its natural order and come up to-morrow evening with out any motion.

maintopic: THE ALBERT AND MONCTON RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It is the private Bills ahead of this one that will prevent its being considered to-morrow. We have only one hour. It would only take a minute to pass this Bill.	.

maintopic: THE ALBERT AND MONCTON RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not opposed to the Bill; I am only drawing attention to what I think is the commencement of a bad nractice.

speechtext: How is it that the House is moved into Committee of the Whole on this Bill now before we have reached the orders of the day? I have seen a number of articles of late regarding the proposal to annex the Bahama Islands to the Dominion of Canada, and some, what I should regard as strong reasons why it would be advisable to do so. The people of the Bahama

Islands appear to be especially anxious that it should be done, for their legislature, I notice, have passed a resolution to that effect. I would like to asic the government if they have had any representations on the subject from their legislature and, if so, if the government have given the matter sufficient consideration to take the House into their confidence, and tell us what they propose to do, if anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are aware, as my hon. friend has pointed out, by the general representations in the press, of a desire in the Bahama Islands to open negotiations with Canada. I think I am correct in stating that we have had no official negotiations on the subject. What has happened is that several enterprising citizens of Canada, residents, I think, of Montreal, who have been visiting the Bahamas, have taken a very warm interest in the matter, and m that way a good deal has been heard of it in the Canadian press. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) asked a question a day or two ago on the subject, and I said that while I did not think there was any official correspondence on the subject I thought it not unlikely that during the visit of the Prime Minister to England it might be the subject of conversation between the colonial office authorities and himself. I think I am quite correct in stating that we have had nothing official on the subject. I should have made a further search of the records, but I am pretty certain I am correct. If I find there is any official communication I will be glad to have it brought down to-morrow.
I would think that there should be some when their legislature has passed a resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am quite sure there has been nothing but what has already appeared in the public press. There have been no negotiations whatever on the subject. It is a matter which might engage attention in the future.

I understood that, while it has been reported in the press that the legislature passed the resolution alluded to, it had not come in an official form to the attention of the government up to the time that the Minister, of Finance made his statement on the subject to the House a few days ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will ask the Secretary of State to make a further examination. It is possible that the resolution has been officially communicated. I would like to ask the hon. acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lemieux) if he has an answer to the question I put yesterday.

I was just going to rise to give my hon. friend the answer which has been communicated to me by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and which is as follows:
With reference to the telegram which Mr. Crocket read in the House to-day, to the effect that the Department of -Marine and Fisheries had notified the collector of customs at Dalhousie not to collect pilotage on vessels carrying pulpwood from Dalhousie to Portland, Maine, -the facts are these:
Early this spring the department was appealed to for a ruling as to whether a vessel carrying pulpwood from Dalhousie to Portland, Maine, was obliged to pay pilotage dues in the pilotage district of Dalhousie. The reply was to the effect that such a vessel came within the list of exempted vessels named in section 477 (c) (iii) of the Canada Shipping Act, which reads as follows:
'Ships propelled wholly or in part by steam employed in voyages between any port or ports in the said provinces-Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island- or any of them and the port of New York, or any port of the United States of America, on the Atlantic north of New York were exempted^ ships.' .
The Bill now before parliament to amend the Canada Shipping Act retains this clause. It is, however, proposed to give the power to every pilotage district to say what ships in the list of exempted ships shall be exempted iu so far as that particular pilotage district is concerned. Any pilotage by-law varying such list of exempted vessels would, of course, be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. It will thus be seen that if this amendment to the Canada Shipping Act passes it will be -competent for every pilotage district to regulate this matter in such a manner as is best suited to its own requirements.

Would the minister state why this- matter is placed in the hands of the collector of customs? Is it usual for the collector -of customs to collect pilotage dues in a pilotage district? It is usually done by the pilotage authority, but this telegram states that the collector of customs has this matter in hand.
I could not say exactly. It is a matter quite new to me, but I will get more information and communicate it to my hon. friend early in the day.
I presume it will be a question of the collector clearing the vessel, and I take it that it has allowed the vessel to clear without payment of the pilotage dues under that section of the law.
That is not the way the telegram read.

Has the Minister of the Interior any information concerning the report which has been widely circulated in the press that a certain transportation company or some immigration agents in the United Kingdom, have by means of advertisements or other public announcements been seeking to bring, about the immigration of young women, using as an inducement the representation that there were husbands in plenty waiting for them, more particularly in the western country. I am quite aware that this is a matter that perhaps lends itself to a more or less facetious treatment, that it has, in fact, been treated in that way by some newspapers but it has a very serious side. Such an action if even in appearance sanctioned by the government might lead to very false impressions and possibly mislead some not overwise young women into coming into this country with anticipations that were fated not to be realized. This has formed the subject of very^ serious consideration amongst organizations in Montreal and other places which concern themselves with taking care of young women immigrants on their arrival in the country and endeavouring to protect them. These ladies think it is a matter that ought to be officially cleared up, that it must be quite understood that no one on behalf of this government or no transportation company, at least with the countenance of the government, should be permitted to hold out inducements of that kind to young women who might be misled thereby and might, on coming to this country, be ex-Mr. DANIEL.
posed to very serious temptations, which these organizations seek to protect them against.
Is this in anticipation of the amendment to the Bank Act by my friend from East Grey?
I do not understand that bank clerks are held out as especially desirable husbands.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No inducement such as this has been held out by the government or any officers of the government with the knowledge of the government, and if it can be brought to the knowledge of the government that any of _ these officials have held out the inducement that my hon. friend has spoken of, I can guarantee that the connection of these officials with the government will cease there and then. I have some knowledge of the rumour referred to. I think it arose from some advertising said to have been done by the Canadian Northern or some of their agents, but while I am not able to give any particular details at the moment, my impression is that on inquiry being made of the Canadian Northern Company they absolutely repudiated any action of that kind and placed the blame where it is very frequently placed, on the newspapers, and intimated their belief that it was a misinterpretation of an interview to give occasion for a startling headline. No such announcements or statements have appeared recently, which would indicate that this was done without authority and that the practice, if it existed, has been checked.

Has the minister had any communication from a Miss Wileman who has been organizing the bringing out of domestic servants to this country? It appears that Miss Wileman before leaving for England had some understanding with the minister and according to the advice I have, the minister promised to give her all the assistance he could in the home immigration office but has failed to make good his promise. Therefore she has been detained over there with the domestic servants whom she had ready to bring to Canada. Has the minister had any communication with or made any promise to the lady which he has not fulfilled.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have had letters from a Miss Wileman, and she has discussed immigration matters with me. She said that her purpose was to bring out domestic servants. I told her that the government could not make any special grants to her for that purpose, that if she wished to engage in that effort she would be subject to the same conditions, and considerations as anybody else. She has no promise of any consideration from me as far

as her work in the old country is concerned. The only promise she had from me was that if she could make arrangements here in Ottawa for the proper entertainment, and care of young women who were brought out by her as domestic servants, I would consider the bearing of some part of the special expense thereby incurred in their entertainment, and care on their arrival here. Beyond that she has ho promise, and never had any from me.
Bill (No. 220) to incorporate the Albert and Moncton Railway Company-Mr. Emmerson.

House in committee on Bill (No. 197) to amend the Railway Act.-Mr. Graham.
On section 4,

This section is absolutely necessary in some form for the purpose of meeting the state of law as found by the Supreme Court of Canada in a recent decision, and with the principle of the section I am in entire accord. It has been found by a majority decision of the Supreme Court that where railway lands are not expropriated, but where a registration of a plan takes place, thus declaring the lands to be subject to the Expropriation Act, the railway company can practically wait forever without taking any other proceedings. The only suggestion I would make is to insert in the third line of subclause (b), after the word 'sanction,' the words, 'whether made before or after the passing of this Act.' Otherwise the effect of this section would be to make one law for the owner, and another for another, because it would mean that this remedy would apply onlv to orders sanctioning the location of the right of way made after the passing of this Act, and would not be any benefit to the people who are affected by an order made before the passing of this Act.
From my standpoint, I do not see any objection to the proposed amendment; but I would like to hear some legal view as to whether or not it would wrongly affect cases that are now pending.

It is the legal effect which I have in my mind. The order referred to granting the sanction, is the order of the board which has located the right of way, and therefore allows the railway company to register their plan which covers the land through which the railway passes, and the registration prevents the owner from selling. Whether the order sanctioning the taking of the land and the locating of the right of way is made before or after the 296	,	'"1

passing of this Act, no railway company can be hurt by this provision, because in either case the owner should have the right which this section contemplates to apply to the Board to have the railway company say w'hether they are really going to take the land or abandon it.

I see no objection to the proposed amendment.
Amendment of Mr. Lancaster agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 7,
Section 235 of the principal Act is amended by striking out the words 'the railway' at the commencement of the said section and substituting therefor the words, 'Subject to the company making such compensation to adjacent or abutting landowners as the board deems proper, the railway of the company '

This section was left over until I would consult concerning it. It was feared it might give cause to litigation, but after close scrutiny, it appears to me that it will have the opposite effect. It merely provides that when a railway asks to go on the highway opposite a man's property, the board may say:	You must pay this man so much
damages or you cannot go there. The damages will be appraised by the board who have every facility to do so.

The only objection is that you make the board both judges and arbitrators I am not afraid of the board abusing its jurisdiction, but I question whether we should give them the right not only to say that damages must be paid but determine the amount.

If a railway runs through a man's land, there is a provision for arbitration, but in this case it does not run through its land, and- the board will only grant its application on the condition of its paying this man a certain amount of damages. The clause is drafted in the handwriting of the chairman of the board, and he thinks this would be an expeditious way of settlement. Heretofore there was no provision to meet a case of the kind; and as the land did not belong to any one, the question of damages was a difficult and litigious one. Damages may accrue. Sometimes a road might run between a man's house and his barn but not on his land, and the chairman thought it would be wise to let the board make the payment of damages a condition. It would be right to empower the board to determine whether a man was entitled to damages or not, but as to the quantum of damages, why should you ask the board to sit as arbitrators?

You are going to make this a board of arbitration as well as a board for administering the Railway Act, It will
edition	,

have to take evidence and sit as a court of law to determine the amount of damages and decide on legal points involved in the question of damages.

This will facilitate the determining of the location. The railway may adopt that location, but only conditional on its paying the compensation fixed by the board. If you adopt this plan you have to pay damages to this individual. They may say: We do not go there. Besides that, in all these cases of expropriation the speediest is the best manner. Why should the party have to go to arbitration? He applies to the commission, they can determine the matter just as well as a board of arbitration. I think it is more to the interest of the party who is affected, and it is an extension of the principle which has not been in the Act at all, because unless a man's property is touched he has no claim for damages. It is an extension of that privilege. I think the plan proposed under the Act is the best.

It is an arbitration, whether that arbitration is conducted by a board or by somebody else. There are some cases where it would be advantage-bus to have t!he question determined by the board. Take, for instance, a case where there could be no doulbt as to the damages, where it is an easy question which would not involve the hearing of many witnesses. That would be a case for the board to decide. But these cases are not very numerous. When it comes to indirect damages, where you do not touch a man's property, it is a difficult question to decide, difficult because you have to get a technical class of evidence, and that involves a number of witnesses. It means either that you have to bring a host of witnesses to Ottawa, or it means that the board have to go out, we will say to Calgary, or some other remote place, and that would involve a good deal of trouble. I think, on the whole, it would be wiser to leave the question of the 'amount of damages to be decided in the ordinary way by expropriation. I do not myself see the necessity of the board coming in at all. I think we might adopt an amendment something like this:	' Without prejudice to the right of a party affected to recover such compensation as he is entitled to.' Then the order might be made for them to go on. If the board is to intervene at all then I think it would be well to let the chairman of the board decide whether there should be compensation, and let the amount of compensation be determined in the ordinary way. But it could be done without the board intervening at all, and the order should be made subject to the right of the party to obtain Mr. LANCASTER.
such compensation as would be fair under the circumstances.
By this Act we are giving them a new right. As _ the law of Canada now stands, it gives him no right of action except where he is injuriously affected.

That is the ease at present, because there is no provision at all for compensation. But here we make a provision, and say that they shall have the * right to go over the highway, but he shall have the right to compensation. All he can get in any case is whatever damages he has sustained. If he does not sustain any damage, he cannot get any, whether we have this provision or not. I am pointing out that we can either leave it for the board to determine whether he shall have compensation or not, or leave it solely to the arbitrators. But if the system pursued here is that the board should intervene, and if they do intervene, the utmost right we should give the board is to say whether he shall have compensation, and leave the amount of compensation to be determined afterwards by arbitration.

I agree with my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) that it is very much better to allow the board to determine what damages the party who is injured shall have. The board, in the first place, have to determine whether it is desirable to allow the railway to run upon the highway at the particular point asked for. The board would naturally take into consideration whether it is going seriously to injure the land owner or not, or whether it might not be better to compel the company to take some other route. Now, is it not much better for the land owner that the board should settle the damages as a condition of granting the _ privileges? The whole matter is determined then by a tribunal which is as competent as you could possibly have. If the suggestion of my hon. friend is acted upon, the company might be permitted to go on and build its railway on a highway, and the adjoining owner would be obliged to go to court, perhaps, and go from court to court, and obliged to incur great expenses before he could get redress. I think it is infinitely preferable that the matter should be settled by the board, and that the amount of damages which they find is reasonable shall be paid before the company is allowed to build its railway.

When I drew the attention of the minister last night to the wording of the amendment, I did not express any opinion as to what would be the better course. I simply pointed out that it would give the board not only the right to determine as to whether a man

is entitled to damages, tout also to determine the quantity. I am inclined to think that, as the matter will have to be gone into very thoroughly to determine, first of all, whether a man is entitled to any damages, and as they have to have the evidence before them, it would take but little more time for them to go a little further and determine the quantity of damages. Therefore, under the circumstances, as the board is a perambulating board, and as it is their custom to make a view of the premises, I think they would be able to ascertain in a summary manner, and with 'less expense, not only the right to damage, but the amount thereof.

It occurs to me, with all respect to the opinion of others who have expressed themselves contrary to my view, that in this legislation there ought to be [DOT]uniformity. The Eailway Act has recognized all through it the principle of arbitration in settling compensation for damages caused to an owner by reason of the railway. That seems to be the principle that has been adopted by this parliament, and has been in vogue for a very long time. Now, if this clause, as proposed, goes into effect, there would be a new jurisdiction, a new court appointed having jurisdiction over this particular matter, which is not in uniformity with the other provisions of the Act. A great deal of difficulty has arisen by reason of legislation in that direction and along that line heretofore. *My hon. friend from Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel) proposes to offer an amendment to this present Act covering the point I am about to mention in regard to farm crossings, and in regard to fences along farms. A serious question has been before the courts a number of times as to whether they have jurisdiction over this question, or whether it must be settled by an arbitration, or whether the Board of Eailway Commissioners alone have jurisdiction to 'order the construction of a crossing, and the payment of damages in consequence of not having provided a farm crossing, or fences, and that sort of thing.
It has been before the courts a great many times in the province of Quebec, I think I am correct in saying, six or seven judges have decided one way, while five have decided the other way, and the Supreme Court has decided with the five. The conflict of authority arises from the want of clear language expressing the jurisdiction and the want of uniformity in jurisdiction. It seems to me that this parliament, having adopted the principle of arbitration in settling damages or compensation in the majority of such cases, ought to folow it in this case. And there are otheT reasons. It would be a great inconvenience if parliament required persons 296i
claiming compensation under this Act to go before the Board of Eailway Commissioners. I think the Act should .be amended in such a way as was suggested by me yesterday-so that the railway company, or the person claiming damages or compensation should have the right to call in a board of arbitration to settle the amount of damages. That procedure is inexpensive, speedy and convenient. The damages may be very small, and it is not well to	incur the expense of
bringing witnesses to where the board is sitting. It seems most desirable that the jurisdiction should be given to one body to try these questions of damages for compensation, so that there may be no conflict of authority, and no question where the person aggrieved should seek a remedy.

It seems to me absolutely necessary that the commission should decide whether damages have been incurred or not. But if the commission decide that there are damages, I think it is not going much further to give thenj power to decide the amount of the damages. I do not know whether these arbitrations are final
Under $600 there is no appeal.

But in some cases there is an appeal to a court. That is wrong; the decision should be final. 1 think it would be better to leave the whole thing to the commission, but, in any case, they should have the absolute right to decide whether there is damage or not.

We all seem to agree that we are going to leave the board to decide whether the owner has right of action or not. That is not determined by the board in ordinary cases. If in this case we are going to allow the board to decide whether there is a right of action, they must necessarily go to a lot of trouble to Teach a reasonable decision. It seems fair that this trouble and expense should be used to ascertain the amount of damages. If the Eailway Commission were a body sitting in Ottawa to which all cases would have to be brought, I would have some hesitation in allowing them authority to assess the damages. But, in deciding whether there is damage or not they would probably view the premises, and at the same time could ascertain the amount of damages.

If the suggestion of the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Mid-dlebro) is carried out, the Eailway Board will have to adopt a different procedure from that which they adopt in cases in which they act, but do not settle the amount of damages. The board sends its engineer, and he makes a report. I have

had a good many cases, and I do not recall any case in which the commissioners visited the locality except in the case of one very dangerous crossing at Grimsby which had killed eight or ten people. Moreover, to adopt the proposal made is to throw upon the board an entirely new set of duties-directing them to decide damages without appeal. In cases over $600 at present there is an appeal from the board of arbitrators to the Superior Court of the province. This is because where the damages are relatively large, legal questions are often involved, and it is felt that either party to the case should have the opportunity to go before the courts. But there is no appeal under $600. In the cases covered by this section the damages may be very serious. The whole frontage benefits of a man's property may be destroyed by the railway running along the highway. The commissioners ought to view the locality in order to settle the amount of damages. But, if these new duties were thrown upon them, they might interfere with the performance of duties which are more important, and which are thrown upon them by the present law. The commissioners might say in a certain case-they could do it legally:	We will not take time to look
at this place, but we will give $1,000 damages no matter what the damages may be; we cannot be bothered going into it any further. That is what might take place The board is a busy one. It has more work piled on it than it can do. No one would have suggested to establish a Board of Railway Commissioners for such purpose as assessing these damages. I might favour giving them these duties if they had not enough to do, but they are likely to be busy enough attending to matters that properly come to them in the administration of the General Railway Act. I believe that if we go the length of declaring that the board shall decide whether damages are recoverable or not, that is as far as we should go. The fixing of the damages should be left under the arbitration clauses. I think the bon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) has well explained that the same principle should apply in these cases of damages as in others. The amount of damages should be settled locally, where the evidence is thorough, and the expense of collecting it is small. Otherwise injustice will be done by compelling people to meet the commission in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, or elsewhere where they may'be sitting, which may be at a considerable distance from the locus in quo. The more I think of it the more I think that the damages should be assessed and decided according to arbitration under the Railway Act.

There are a great many ordinary arbitration cases with a certain Mr. LANCASTER
method of procedure arising every day with railways. The cases that will arise under this section are very few indeed; in fact, up to date, nobody has any damages that will accrue under this section.
But they would have had if this section had been the law.

I think that everybody will agree that the number of cases will be very small in which there will be any damages. Let me read the section of the Act:
The railway may be carried upon, along or across any existing highway upon leave therefor having been first obtained from the board as hereinafter authorized.
They must get leave first to go upon, along, or across the highway.
Provided that the board shall not grant leave to any oounpany to carry any street railway or tramway, or -any railway operated or to be operated .as a street railway or tramway, along any highway which is within the limits of any city or incorporated town, until the company has first obtained consent therefor by a by-law of the municipal authority of such city or incorporated town.
2.	The company shall, before obstructing any such highway by its works, turn the highway so as to leave an open and good passage for carriages, and, on completion of the works, restore the highway to as good a condition as nearly as passible as it originally had.
3.	Nothing in this section shall deprive any such company of rights conferred upon it by any special Act of parliament of Canada, or amendment thereof, passed prior to the 12th day of March, 1903.
These are the conditions under which the board may allow a company to use the streets. But here arises another condition: John Smith has some property. The property over which the railway goes is on the public highway, and it, therefore, does not belong to John Smith, but he says:	It
is going to hurt me if you allow the railway to be placed there. The board will say: We find that is so, and they can say to the company: You may go there provided you compensate John Smith. The damage amounts to so much.
Would not an arbitration assess the damage?

Yes, but it may be assessed there before it gets into the courts. The railway company, if it has to go into the courts, cannot tell whether they can go along that highway on reasonable terms or not. It is in the interest of everybody that there should be speed in the matter, and the railway companies say:	We cannot
afford to go upon the highway on those terms, and we will take a location in some other place. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred it can be settled in twenty-four hours. Looking at it from the practical

standpoint it will tend to keep men out of expensive lawsuits, to secure them fair damages, and enable the railway to be built within a reasonable time.
That is the objection to your Bill.

I agree with what the minister has said, that it will be more speedy, but speediness is not right if the amount is not correct. It is not justice to a man to get a speedy decision, if the decision is not for the right amount.
He loses it in costs.

If you want to hurry up the decision you can have it done in a month. The railway company must give ten days' notice, the property owner has either to accept or decline the offer and, if he declines it, they can go before the county judge and get the arbitrators appointed.
Then there might be delay.

If it can be decided in a month what would that amount to? It is the speediness of the matter that I am afraid of. It might be that the board would say: We must hurry up and make this order, and they would issue an order for $1,000 or $500, which might be too much or might not be enough. They just guess at it. It is done by explosion, they do not understand it, and I think it should be done properly. The land owner, as a rule, is a poor man, and the case should be decided in the interests of both parties in a proper way. There would not be much delay because, if the railway made a fair offer, it would be accepted, and it would be all over in ten days. If it made an unfair offer and it was submitted to arbitration, it would be all over in a month, and justice would be done, instead of the thing being jumped at.

There would be a very great deal of force in the contention that we ought to have uniformity in the tribunal that is to assess damages in all cases of taking property by railways were it not for one thing. That is that we are dealing here essentially with an exceptional case. Where the matter goes to arbitration, and where the law absolutely settles the right to damages, the one question to be submitted is, how much ought to be paid. As the law stands at present the property owner, where the railway runs on the highway, has no rights. It is proposed to give him a right not absolutely established by law, hut a right conditional upon the judgment of the Railway Commission. It would be a very inconvenient system to leave it to the Railway Commission to absolutely determine whether this
man should have any damages or not and then proceed to another tribunal to establish how much they were. You may arrive at this result that the other tribunal may determine that this man is entitled to damages of a class that the Railway Commission never meant he should be entitled to. The Railway Commission have the determination of whether this man should get damages. There must be present to their judgment and mind some idea, not necessarily of the precise amount, but of the nature of the things for which he ought to be compensated. For instance, it might be that his access to the highway is interfered with. That is one ground upon which they might determine that he should get compensation. But if they merely say that he should get compensation, and send it to a board of arbitration, that board might assess the damages on some other basis, for instance, because his house is shaken, or for some other reason, which the Railway Commission never intended should be taken as the basis for assessing damages. And if they had foreseen that that was going to be the result, they might, in their judgment, have thought that giving the land owner damages for all injuries of that kind, would be a greater injustice to the railway than giving them damages generally. As the landowner's right depends on the judgment of the Railway Commission, one of the essential factors which must operate in leading them to a conclusion is what kind of damages he is to get, what the extent of the damages is to be; and to ask them to determine in an abstract way simply that he is entitled to damages of some kind, and then send it off to some one else to determine the amount of damages, is creating a situation where you make it exceedingly difficult for the Railway Commission to come to a conclusion on the question.
In the second place, you run the risk that the Railway Commission may say: You do this subject to compensating so and so, and the Board of Arbitration might think there was no damage at all. Thus you would have two tribunals arriving at contrary conclusions. Of course, that is not likely to occur, as boards of arbitration generally are disposed to grant compensation, and rightly so, perhaps, as the railway is disturbing the property of the man. In view of these considerations, it would be safer to adhere to the Act as proposed. By this Act, we are improving the position of the proprietor of adjacent lands; as it stands to-day he gets nothing. Would it not be wise to pass the Act as it now stands, leaving the whole matter to the determination of the Railway Commissioners? The proprietor advances to the extent that he gets to a state of affairs where he can obtain compensation. If it is found in prac-

tice that this does not work satisfactorily with regard to fixing the quantity of damages, it would be possible to remedy it; and if, on the other hand, it should be found to work out satisfactorily, it would obviate a great deal of complication, and in that case, I think, it would be desirable to adhere to it. On the whole, I think that the wise course would be to leave the Bill as it stands.

With all respect to the hon. gentleman from Montreal, (Mr. Doherty), it seems to me there is a contradiction in terms when one reads the provisions of this Act. The hon. member seems to think that the board must determine the question first as to whether or not there is any right to compensation, and then that the arbitrators should say what the amount of that compensation is to be. It seems to me that that contradicts the provisions of the clause as here proposed. The clause, according to its fair reading, declares that where a railway crosses a highway there shall be a right to compensation, it is just a question of the amount. This parliament declares that there shall be a right to compensate, that is already decided by statute. The board would have no.right to say: Well, yes, the owner shall have compensation. The statute says that already, so that when the argument is used that the board must determine whether or not there is a right to compensation, it is contradicting the statute. Assuming that the owner is entitled to some compensation, there is no reason why the railway company should not be able to determine that just as speedily as they determine the compensation they shall pay for the lands of an owner taken in any other way. They can serve their notice on him and make their offer, and if it is not accepted they can go to arbitration in the ordinary way. I would suggest that we strike out the words ' as the board may deem proper.' Then you will have the whole thing covered by one court, and the right court.

We cannot very well agree to this provision, as it is suggested, and I would suggest that this section also be allowed to stand over, so that we may consider it further and deal with it with the other amendments which the minister will bring in after we reassemble.

I think, too, that section 11, which will be very contentious, should either stand over or be dropped. It is undoing what it took us three strenuous years to accomplish here for the owners of animals in this country. It is absolutely retrograde legislation, it is putting us back where we were in 1900, when I first came here. Many members will remember that a commission was appointed in connection with legislation introduced by myself, and Mr. DOHERTY.
the House finally determined unanimously upon a principle of law which should protect the owners of animals killed by railways. The minister, who was not m the House at the time, perhaps does not realize that the effect of section 11 is to undo that legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman is addressing himself to section 11, while other hon. members desire to speak to section 7.
I wish to show why the committee should rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no motion to that effect. I think the hon. gentleman should wait until section 7 is disposed of.

I am very much disposed to agree that under the old section 235 the land owner has no right, and that the purport of this section 7 is under certain circumstances to create a right in the owner. The body that creates the right is the Railway Board, and the body that creates the right should determine its value, if the section remains as it is. But it seems to me that it was a great mistake to destroy the common law right of the owner by section 235. The power should never have been given to a railway to pass upon a highway without compensating the adjoining owners for the damage done to their property. That power was given by section 235, and, therefore, the common law right of the owner to compensation was taken away. It seems to me that right should be restored, and the compensation to be allowed to the owner for the invasion of that right should be left to the ordinary tribunal of arbitration. My suggestion would be to amend section 235 so as to preserve the common law right of the adjoining owners when the railway passes along the highway, and then let section 7 specify the tribunal which shall determine the compensation after that is done.

This clause seems to me to be so much in the interests of the people that I hesitate to drop it unless some good reason is given. The situation at present is that a man's property may be damaged by a railway running along the highway, and he has no recourse. By this section we propose to give him recourse. The clause appears to me to be so simple that I do not like to take the responsibility of dropping it. I would be perfectly willing to accept the suggestion that its consideration be delayed if the committee so desires.

Why not adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for West Hastings, and simply declare the railway company liable to pay damages and not

bother the hoard with the matter at all? It is not the function of the Railway Board to determine whether or not there is an evil in the country that requires redress. It is for this parliament to take the responsibility of declaring that if a man's land is damaged in the way the section describes, he should have compensation, and then let the arbitration clause of the Railway Act settle the amount. I do not see why the board should be brought into the matter at all. They are not properly assessors as to land damages, nor law makers to say that the principle of land damages should be applied. This is the function of parliament. With regard to this provision causing litigation, there is just as much evil in litigation before the board as before the courts, and in my opinion litigation in the ordinary way is more expeditious than litigation before the Railway Board.

I want to add another reason why there should be some little modification. As I pointed out a moment ago, this section deprives a land owner of a right which ought to be restored, and it gives the Railway Board the power to create a right. In the first place, the common law right is destroyed, and then a new right is given. The Board of Railway Commissioners are given the absolute right of determining the value which is a big power to put in its hands. I do not want the Bill withdrawn because it is an improvement on the law, but I want the common law aright restored to the land owner, and leave the assessment of damages to the tribunal provided by the Act.

I want to see this section withdrawn, because if we pass it now, we shall never get it into proper shape. The Finance Minister made a very reasonable proposition last night when he suggested that clauses, which involve diversity of opinion, might be left in abeyance until we meet again. On section 10,

This is a section we had a good deal of discussion about. Subsection 5 deals with the case where a railway is being constructed through inclosed land, and animals escape from such inclosed land upon the property of the company. I said last night that this clause had been practically agreed to by consultation with the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the farmers' deputations from the west intimated that it met their views. What was agreed to was the whole 'section, except the words at the end ' upon the property of the company.' Then after that was agreed to, it was suggested by the farmers' organization that there ought to be something put in to make a railway company responsible for the destruction of crops as well. But this did not quite meet with the view of the committee. Last night we were discussing how to reach that point. I had a clause prepared by the legal department which did not quite_ meet the views of the committee last night, and they thought there might be some improvement in it. This was the clause I proposed last night, and hon. gentlemen who know the situation in the west will see what I was trying to get at. This is what I .proposed:
Where a railway is being constructed through inclosed land it shall be the duty of of the company to take effective measures to prevent cattle or other animals escaping from or getting upon such inclosed lands, or upon the property of the company, by reason of any act or thing done or permitted to he done by the company.
It is contended that by making it obligatory upon the company to prevent animals

from getting on land or in getting off land, they would be responsible for damage done to crops on the land as well as responsible for the killing of cattle who got off the land on to the property of the railway company. In discussing it this morning with my legal department again, I pointed out that the question raised in committee last night was that some officer or agent of the company might do something, such as a contractor, that would allow damage to be done, and under the clause as we had it the railway could not be held liable. I think the member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) said he was not clear whether these words would not be open to that construction or not, and it was thought desirable in a case of that kind to make clear just what the liability would be where a contractor or some official was concerned, because, as he pointed out, the railway company might issue instructions to any of its agents that they must keep the fences closed, and if they did not, then it would be open to the construction that the company had done their part and would not be liable.
If contractors are there with their permission they ought to be responsible.

I do not think there would be much difficulty about an agent, but the difficulty is in the case of an independent contractor, with whom the railw'ay company have made a contract to build a certain section of road, and has stipulated with him that he shall attend to the fences and carry out all the obligations. It is in that ease that there might be difficulty about its being held that any acts of his which brought about any violation of his contract, and which brought about damage to outsiders, was an act permitted by the company.
That is what I understood. Well, would it be right for us to make the company liable for the action of an independent contractor?
He is there with their permission.
If a contractor performs an act in violation of his contract with the railway company, should the company be liable?

I think in that case the railway company ought to be liable, for this reason, that they are given a right to construct that railway, and it is quite proper that we should put upon them the obligation of seeing that the construction of that railway does no damage to an outsider; if we start by doing that, the company have no right to claim that they can throw off that obligation on to the shoulders of a contractor They might come to the contractor
to be indemnified for any damage they may have had to pay. But after all, the source of damage to the individual is the exercise by the railway company of its power of constructing this railway. Whether it does it by itself or by another, it would be just that it should be responsible to the outsider for damage caused by the construction of their road.
The question is not whether they ought or ought not to be liable; it is whether the words of the Act cover the case.

They should be liable, but they would have redress against the contractor. Like a corporation which is obliged to keep the sidewalks in repair, when they permit a contractor to tear up the sidewalks the municipality will still remain liable for damage to persons injured. Let the company put in a clause to indemnify the contractor. They should have redress against the contractor, but they should be liable to the injured persons.

We all agree that somebody ought to be liable, and it seems to me it ought to be the company. I propose these words to cover the case:
Where a railway is being constructed through inclosed land it shall be the duty of the company to take effective measures to prevent cattle or other animals escaping from or getting upon such inclosed lands, or upon the property of the company, by reason of any act or thing done by the company, its contractors, agents or employees.

That is still open to the objection of the hon. member for St. Anne (Air. Doherty) that the company might make all sorts of agreements with the contractor to protect themselves from damage. The company should be liable the same as a private individual. If a private individual enters my property through a contractor, he is liable for the action of the contractor.

Let me read what was agreed upon as likely to meet the situation, and then I will read my amendment:
Where	a	railway	is	being	constructed
through inclosed land it shall be the duty of the company to take effective measures to prevent cattle and other animals escaping from such inclosed lands.
Those were the words approved of after a good deal of discussion. Now it is said that that would not protect the crop, and, therefore, I have replied with this section:
Where	a	railway	is	being	constructed
through inclosed lands, it shall be the duty of the company to take effective measures to prevent cattle or other animals escaping from or getting upon such inclosed lands, or upon the property of the company, by reason of any

act or thing done by the company, its contractors, agents or employees.
Why not make it all damages without enumerating grain, stock, &c.?

I want to adhere to what seems to be satisfactory to all the people most intimately interested in it. I am making it, if anything, stronger than they had it, and I do not want to go too far the other way.
Is it the intention of the minister that the railway company shall be liable for all damages caused by the railway company, passing through inclosed fields, to grain, cattle or any other property?

Why, say anything about cattle or wheat? Why not say:
Where the railway is being constructed through inclosed fields, the railway company shall be liable for all damage caused to the owner by the company, its contractors, subcontractors, servants or agents.
It will be ordinarily subject to all damages it might cause, I imagine. .
I do not think that is as strong as the minister's proposal.

I would propose that the subsection be changed to read as follows:
Where the railway is being constructed through inclosed lands, it shall be the duty of the company to take effective measures to prevent cattle or other animals escaping from or getting upon such inclosed lands or upon the property of the company by reason of any act or thing done by the company, its contractors, agent9 or employees.
Should yon not also say ' or any act omitted to be done '? There are two classes of negligence there are omissions and commissions.

I discussed that pretty thoroughly with my legal department today, and they convinced me by legal arguments that everything would be the act of the railway company in producing a condition that did not before exist, and that it would all come under this section.

It would be quite a burden on the railway which would require them to take effective steps, because effective steps must mean steps that Will effectively prevent any damages. I do not see how you could make it any stronger.

The obligation, no doubt, is to take effective measures to prevent any damage resulting from any act done. If the damage results merely from Mr. GRAHAM.
the omission to take effective measures you will not be able to bring suit based on any act that the railway company did to cause that damage. The damage will be caused because they did not do something.
Give us a case.
Suppose the fences are not up, and they omit to put them up.
If the fences are not up it is because the contractors have knocked them down. This applies to inclosed lands.
Suppose they are accidentally knocked down. I cannot at the moment lay my finger upon a particular case of omission in this instance.
Supposing there is a whirlwind?

Yes, supposing these fences are carried off by force majeure, and the contractor omits to reconstruct them. Suppose he comes through a gate and leaves it open, he does not open the gate but he just leaves it open. The damage is caused because he omits to close it. In most legislation that I haye seen of this kind provision is made for acts of omission.
Supposing the fence is destroyed by a whirlwind the company would be liable for not taking effective measures to prevent whirlwinds.

Not to prevent whirlwinds. Underneath all law there lies the commonsense principle that a man is not responsible for a force majeure; hut if the fence has been destroyed by a whirlwind the company are not responsible for the destruction of the fence, but they become bound to put up a new fence, because that would necessarily be an effective measure, and if you undertake to sue them you will not be able to show that by any act they caused the damage; the act was the act of God, but still they would be responsible for the replacing of the fence.

Take the case of a whirlwind which destroys a fence. The section speaks of a property which is inclosed. The railway company has nothing to do with property which is not inclosed. It does not touch it, and it is not responsible in any way.
Suppose the fence is destroyed by fire?
If the railway company has not taken the fence down it has nothing to do with it. It has not made any change in the condition.
If it is not put up by them would it not be an act of omission?

If it did not come within the purview of where they were operating they would have nothing to do with it. I went through this for an hour with my legal department, and they convinced me that this would meet every condition where a railway could possibly be held to be liable.
What would the minister say of the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), where the gate is left open? Would that be an omission?

The next section says that the company shall be liable unless where the gate is left open by some person outside of its employees. The case of a gate being left open is fully covered by another section.

If we are going to pass this section, I would say that the limitation should be to the owner of the animal or his servant. We discussed this matter for three years, beginning with 1901. We had a commission appointed especially to deal with this question. They took evidence all over the country and reported to parliament, and finally the legislation of 1903 was passed by the unanimous consent of this House. In the committee I had many warm supporters on the Liberal side of this legislation, when it was being passed, among them the hon. member for South Wellington, and the former member for Haldimand.
The hon. gentleman yesterday said that he was repealing for the benefit of the farmers the clause which says that they shall not allow their animals to be within half a mile of a railway crossing on the public highway, but he is repealing more, he is repealing the clause which puts the onus on the railway to prove that the owner is negligent. The hon. gentleman said that the farmers' associations were in favour of this legislation. With all due deference to the farmers' associations, as a man having actions against railways in c:iees of this kind, I say that the farmers' associations are bringing on themselves interminable litigation to construe this Act. Apparently they do not understand what their rights have been since 1903, if they approve of this. There has been no litigation, the only question has been the amount of damages where they were recoverable, and where they were not recoverable, no attempt has been made to secure them. Any lawyer could tell from the statement of facts whether the company was liable or not, and the railway company also recognized when they were responsible.
The present law is quite clear that the railway company is liable unless they can prove that it was through the fqult or neglect of the owner of the animal or his servant that the animal got on the track, except in cases where the animal was killed on the highway. Why change all that? This is a most drastic taking away of the rights which we, after full consideration during three sessions, granted to the owners of animals. cept his own negligence, and is entitled to recover if the railway company does not prove such negligence.	.	.

I tell the minister, as a lawyer who has a great deal of experience in these cases, who discovered the outrageous state of the law before he got a seat in this House, and who has realized the beneficial results of the change that was accomplished in 1903, and the great saving of expense in litigation consequent upon that change, that this particular section is under the circumstances very hastily entered upon.
