The chairman of the board is very busy, and he would do well to stay busy administering the laws we put up to him to administer, and not-to use an ordinary expression-butt in and tell the minister that he knows the conditions better than the representatives of the people who have to live under the conditions, and who with all deference to the chairman of the board, know what are the practical evils to be remedied and the practical common sense way to meet them from both sides. I appeal to the minister; can he say the farmer's association is well advised in asking for the repeal of subsections 4 and 5? They were well satisfied with the way this Act was working except as to the conditions of which my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), is better able to speak than I, though I know something of them from him. The minister is right in repealing the section in regard to animals on the highway within half a mile of the crossing. But, while he gives the farmers five cents worth in this way, he is taking away $5,000 worth by the repeal of subsections 4 and 5. By doing this, as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie shows, he is taking away the chance of the farmer to recover for his animal killed in this way. 'Subsections 4 and 5 fix on the railway company the onus of proving negligence ' on the part of the owner. Cannot the minister see that these men were ill advised when they asked for a repeal of these subsections? They do not understand. They are like a child of eight or ten years who is asked if he would not like a dollar to buy candy and told all he has to do is to get his guardian to sign away tire farm that will come to him when he is 21 years of age.
In what case were they protected before in which they are now not protected?

If subsection 4 is not repealed here is what we have:
When any horse9, sheep, swine or other cattle at large, whether upon the highway or not, get upon the property of the company and are killed or injured by a train, the owner of any such animal so killed or injured shall except in the cases otherwise provided for by the next following section, be entitled to recover the amount of such loss or injury Mr. LANCASTER.
against the company in any action in any court of jurisdiction,-
The cases provided' for in the following sections are practically the same as are provided here.
-unless the company establishes that such animal got at large through the negligence or wilful act or omission of the owner or his agent, or of the custodian of such animal or his agent.
5. The fact that any such animal was not in charge of some competent person or persons shall not, if the animal was killed or injured upon the property of the company and not at the point of intersection with the highway, deprive the owner of his right to recover.
These put the onus of proof of negligence on the company. It was not a matter of guesswork. The farmer goes out in the morning and finds two of his cattle gone. He does not know how they got away any more than the railway company does. But if these animals are killed at the railway and unless the railway company can prove negligence, the owner can recover damages. The fact that the animal was not in charge of a competent person is not to be taken as proof of negligence. That is a necessary part of it.
Which exceptions let the company out of liability in such cases? I cannot understand how th^y would be relieved.
Under the Act as now proposed?
Yes.

It says:
The company shall be liable to the owner for the full value of all horses, sheep, swine or other cattle that may be injured upon the company's lands through the operations of the railway, save where such killing or injury was caused by reason of any person

Then you enumerate all the cases that will happen, and make each of them an exception. I cannot see how a man can possibly recover on an animal killed on the track unless he can prove that the station master, or somebody else in the employ of the company deliberately admitted the animal to the property of the company.
That is on either side of the railway at a farm crossing.

The animal is not killed unless it gets upon the railway, and the party does not recover except in those cases. Now every one of those clauses provided for every possible case where that animal would get killed, unless it could be proved that, an agent of the company deliberately led the horse or cow upon the railway.
Supposing his cow was at large and strayed on the crossing?

Then he cannot recover simply because he suffered it to go there. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the animal is killed because it goes down the highway to the point of intersection, and gets on the track and is killed on the railway property.
Except as authorized by this Act, -without the consent of the company, riding, leading or driving any animal, or suffering it to enter upon any railway and within the fences and guards thereof.
Except that before, we had this deliberate statement that that alone should not disentitle a man to recover. That before was in the shape of -a liability on the man. No one can doubt what the decision of the courts will be if you repeal subsections 4 and 5, which put the onus upon the company -of proving that the man himself was negligent. Then they don't have to prove anything of the kind. I have no doubt that this Act has been drawn in the interest of the railways, although the minister does not think so.
I cannot see any point where it is in their interest.

None is so blind as those that won't see. I want to point out to him that in the sections that are a protection to the farmer in this regard, the onus is to be on the company to prove him negligent. Surely the minister knows that when these sections are repealed a different construction is to be put upon the sections that remain. I repeat they were adopted by the unanimous consent of this House, and they were sent up to the Senate, who objected to them. We had a conference, and the Senate had to give in. The farmers' associations were thinking of the fact that they were escaping the trouble of having to keep their animals half a mile from the railway crossing, and this section would mislead them into thinking so, because section 294 does s-ay that. I do not -see how this can be construed so that the man can be paid for his animals under ordinary circumstances. But I am certain that it won't apply to nine out of ten cases that it now applies to, because there always will be litigation to ascertain whether he led, or drove the animal, or suffered it to enter upon the railway or within the fences and guards thereof. Now let me suggest to the minister to repeal -subsections 1 and 2 of section 294, and leave subsections 3, 4 and 5. If he does that he will be doing .something for the farmers; if he does not, he will be handing them five cents with one hand and taking away from them five dollars with the other. It is the common law duty of a man to keep his animals at home. Now, unless we declare that the company shall he liable, and if we do not set up against a defence to
such liability what is now being repealed, then -at common law the man would be guilty of negligence for letting his animal get there, although he did not intend it. We are all sincere in desiring to protect the farmers' rights, and the intention of the minister is to increase the protection to the farmers. Therefore, it can be doing n-o harm simply to repeal subsections 1 and 2 of 294, and leave subsections 3, 4 and 5 to stand.

I have been endeavouring to ascertain whether the proposed amendments lessen the liability of the railway company for accidents, and it seems to me that if there is -any difference it increases their liability. I think if we make a comparison of the -law as it was in sections 294 and 295, with the proposed section, which consolidates the two, we will find that in the part which my hon. friend complains of, that is the part where animals are allowed to run at large, the proposed amendment increases: the liability of the company instead of lessening it; in this respect, that under the Act as it exists at present, when animals are running at large and get upon the railway, prima facie the company is responsible. The burden is put upon the railway company to prove that the owner of the animal was guilty either of negligence or of some wilful act with respect to it. The meaning of the present section, I think, is that even if he is guilty of negligence the railway is liable.
' Mr. LANCASTER. No, they are not liable if he suffers it to get there.
i Mr. CLARKE (Essex). Yes. The only way the railway can escape -is by proving that the owner wilfully turned the animal on the railway property. The first two paragraphs of the proposed section II, (a) and (b), are practically the same as they were before. They refer to farm crossings, >and do not refer to animals running at large. Therefore, these are the sections which refer to animals running at large:
The company shall be liable to the owner for the full value of all horses, sheep, swine or other cattle that may be killed or injured upon the company's lands through the operation of the railway.
They state there that they shall be liable .for everything. What is the exception?
Save where such killing or injury is caused by reason of any person-
(d) turning any animal upon or within the enclosure of any railway company.
That is the only exception1 with regard to animals at large. They are liable for all animals save where a person turns an animal upon or within the enclosure of the railway company.
You must read (e) with that.

No, (e) does not Tefer to animals running at large.
. Mr. LANCASTER. Yes, because he suffers it to get there.

I do not think the hon. gentleman quite understands my argument. The old clause was a declaration that a man should not do a certain thing. Section 295 was the clause which declared the company's liability.
Quite so, in the case of animals running at large.
Section 294 was a declaration of liability. Section 295! simply said that a man should not do certain things but that was not a declaration of the liability of the company.

Section 294 is dealing with animals running at large. Section 295 is not dealing with animals running at large,- it is with the question of animals running at large that we are now concerned. Section 294 says that when any animals 'are killed or injured the; owner shall be entitled to recover ' except in the cases otherwise provided.' This section simply says that they shall be liable for all animals unless it be shown that they are deliberately driven upon the railway.
Is not the chief point of difference between the sections, that in the old Act there is an express provision that the company must establish negligence?
Yes, but here they are removing even negligence on the part of the other party.
But it does not say that they must establish it.

It makes no difference whether there is negligence or not; the company is liable. It does not make any exception for negligence of the owner; it only specifies wilfully driving the animals on the property of the railway company.	*

Under the old Act, if I find my cattle killed in the enclosure of the r'ailway company, the company will be liable unless they can establish my negligence. Is there anything in this Act which allows me to take a similar position? There is an express stipulation in the old Act which says that the company must establish negligence. True, this Bill says that the company are liable, but it does not say that they must establish negligence. The old Act declared their liability unless they proved that they were negligent. Under the present Bill there is no express stipulation which says that the company must prove negligence. In that respect I think the farmers have been gold-bricked.

Under the present Act the burden of proof is on the railway company to prove facts which disentitle the owner to relief-negligence or some wilful act. The present section does not, in express terms, say that the burden is upon the railway company to prove that the owner of the animal turned the animal upon *the railway.
Or was guilty of negligence.
There is no question of negligence under the present Bill, because the company is liable whether there is negligence or not.
The question of contributory negligence is always open, and a court would say that ordinary contributory negligence disentitles the claimant to recover.

I do not know about that. Ordinarily, in a case of contributory negligence, you cannot recover, but if the Act says that you shall recover except in a certain instance, you must prove this instance. Whether or not the doctrine of contributory negligence is applicable, that stands upon its own footing, and we are' not concerned with it one way or the other.
I do not know that anybody will say that we ought to put a statute upon the statute-book saying that- contributory negligence or the absence of contributory negligence must be proved by either side.
That is what was done in 1903, and that has been the law up to now.
Not contributory negligence. What you are saying is that they are not liable unless the company prove negligence or some other act on the part of the owner.

We have said that a certain thing would not disentitle a man to recover which would otherwise be con-

tributory negligence. We have said that allowing any animal to run at large shall not disentitle him to recover. We did not say that that should be contributory negligence which should disentitle him.

Would the hon. gentleman have any objection to changing the proposed section so as to say that the following only shall be defences to an action under this section? Then we would know if we had our case proved, and it would lie upon the company to make a defence upon the grounds mentioned in the various subsections.
As to turning the animal upon the property of the company.
Suffering it to get there.

I do not know whether or not it should be amended, but I do not see much need of it for this reason. The only escape from liability is in [DOT]case, there is evidence that the owner of the animal turns it upon the railway. I think it is going pretty far to say that the railway company must prove that the owner turned the animal upon the railway.
That is the law today.

It goes further to-day. It is not a question of negligence. There might be negligence in the way you fasten a gate, or in a hundred other things. That ground of defence is taken away absolutely. The only way i.ne railway company can escape under the proposed amendment is by showing that the owner actually turned the animal upon the railway.
No; suffered it to get there.
That is a different thing entirely.
It says so in paragraph (e).
That is another clause. Under the present clause there is no burden upon the railway company as to suffering an animal to get upon the railway.
Yes.

No. The present Act, section 294, subsections 4 and 5, only refer to animals running at large. Section 295, subsection (3) says that:
Except as authorized by this Act, without the consent of the company, riding, leading or driving any such horse, cattle, or other animal, or suffering the same to enter upon any railway, and within the fences and guards thereof.
There is no burden of proof upon the railway with respect to that.
Mr. LANCASTER But you must read subsection 5 of section 294 of the Act which you are repealing, and which says that the fact that such animal was not in charge of some competent person shall not, if the animal is killed, deprive the owner of the right of recovery. You are taking that away and you might as well read the two together, that is read the present law with that which you are proposing to-day. It is saying that there shall not be contributory negligence.
I cannot read anything in the present Act which casts any onus on them in respect to anything in section 295.
It distinctly says so.

I do not think it is any great hardship. I think it will be going pretty far as the section is to say that before the railway company can succeed, they must prove that the owner of the animal killed, turned it on the highway.
That has been the law since 1903.
In the working out of it any lawyer of experience in these things will say that it amounts to nothing at all. Consider a man going to court
No, they do not go to court.

Whether a man has a genuine claim or not he knows if he turned the animal on the highway. It does not depend on a tramp opening the gate as at present, the only point is that it has to be proved it is there, the company is liable unless somebody shows the man turned it on the highway himself. Then is it any great hardship that a man should have to go there and prove what any honest man should be able to prove without difficulty, that he did not put it on the highway himself?	.
We came to the conclusion that that was not a good argument, the man does not know how the animal got away.

My hon. friend ignores what I said as to the difference between the present Act and the old Act. In the old Act it was not the act of the person himself that was the issue, it might be the act of other people, of any one opening the gate. There you very well said: 'We will not put the onus on the owner to prove that somebody did not open the gate, or did open the gate, we are going to put that onus on the railway, and say



that unless the railway prove there was some negligence or something of that kind, they shall be liable.'
Why change it now?
Because we are striking out the negligence entirely. There is only one thing that exempts the company, and that is if the owner actually turned the animal on the railway himself.

Why not strike out the words ' save where,' in the second line of paragraph 11 so that it would read:
Unless the railway company establish that such killing or injury is caused by reason of

So as to put the onus on them of establishing the exception.

I know that opposition or even comment on this Bill is very likely to be interpreted as opposing the farmers' demands, and consequently a very serious step. Much as I respect the opinion of Mr. Bower and those associated with him, I do not see why we should abdicate our functions in their favour, nor yet in favour of the Chairman of the Railway Commission. We had a committee of the House last year dealing with a proposed amendment to the Railway Act, including an amendment to subsection 4 of 254 which is repealed by this Bill. That committee reported favourably on the amendment which was adopted by the Minister of Railways, and embodied in the law only a year ago. By virtue of that a large class of losses for which there had previously been no compensation, were included in the list of those losses for which a railway is liable. That is now all repealed. What is the explanation?

I argued in favour of that clause in my discussions with representatives of the farmers of the west. I pointed out that clause as assisting them in their own protection. They were unanimous in telling me it did not meet the object at all. In one or two places I had very warm discussions with representatives of the farmers, and they told me that this did not meet the case.
The explanation is the same as formerly, that Mr. Bower did not want it.
It was not Mr. Bower.

Nobody contended that the amendment of last session gave all that was desired. I introduced an amendment this session that went much further, but to say it meant nothing and did not cover cases not previously covered, is to talk nonsense. Under the old law in certain conditions a railway company was Mr. CLARKE (Essex).
liable if it killed or injured horses or cattle. Under the same conditions of negligence it might do other damage besides killing or injuring horses or cattle by trains or engines, but in such cases the railway company was not liable. The courts held, on the theory of the history of the legislation, that the class of damage for which they were liable was confined to the killing of horses or cattle. There is a line of cases leading up to that where serious losses are suffered with no redress. This parliament got to work and remedied that. Now the whole remedy is to be thrown to the winds because a certain gentleman out in Alberta does not understand what it means. This same gentleman had submitted to him the amendment which I introduced this year and he could see nothing in it. I venture to say that any man on this side of the House could submit any amendment in the world to that man and he would see nothing in it. What has been the law in this regard? Up to the present time the law can be stated in very clear and very brief terms. If an animal is killed or injured on the right of way by a train or engine the owner recovers unless the company shows the animal got there by the negligence or wilful act of the owner. It is very true, as the minister says, that conditions are different in the east and in the west, and that the law as it stood remedied conditions in eastern Canada to a much greater extent than in western Canada, because in eastern Canada it would be almost impossible for the company to show that the animal got at large by the negligence or wilful act of the farmer. In western Canada animals run at large almost indiscriminately, in fact a great part of the industry of western Canada would have to collapse unless animals were so allowed to run at large, and as a consequence of their running at large in this way in almost 80 cases out of 100 the railway company were able to show at once that the animal was simply turned out, that it got out of a gate and was running at large on the commons. In four cases out of five the company got an admission from the man himself and they took the precaution generally of getting it by affidavit. When the killing of an animal was reported to them their usual course was to send an affidavit to the poor fellow whose animal was hurt and he filled it out and sent it in and then and there the whole case collapsed, because the animal got out in that way. A gentleman near Portage la Prairie had a band of horses, some one drifted in his gate, got a drink of water, and went away leaving the gate open. The band of horses got out. But it happened that the farmer knew that the gate was open; he was passing

some corner of his farm and saw the gate open. We were compelled to advise that man that he had no case, although his animals were killed by getting on the track through the negligence of the company in not keeping their gates closed. Although the negligence of the company was the clear cause of the loss, the farmer had no case.
This is an improvement on that.

This is no improvement. Whereas before it was a matter of some difficulty to advise the farmer whether he had any cause of action or not, under this Bill he who runs may read and may tell him that he had no cause for action. It has been held that unless you expressly put the burden on the company to prove the exceptions, the burden is on the plaintiff, and he has to negative the exceptions. Previously he did not have to negative them. All he had to show was that the animals were not on the right of way, and the burden was on the company to show that he had let them loose. The state of the law before was not satisfactory, at any rate in western Canada, because the company should have been liable unless they could prove that they were not negligent. It is not hard to frame a statute to meet the case if we simply take the common law of the country, and apply it to the Railway Act; but the railway companies have taken good care that the common law is negatived almost throughout the Act, and it was never more clearly negatived than it is by the amendment now submitted. If we apply the principles of the common law, the result will be that the railway company will be liable for loss if the negligence or breach of the law by the company is the immediate cause of the loss, no matter whether there was a remote cause or not. Let the railway company show that there was no negligence on their part, and then they will escape. That is all that has to be done. I submitted to this House a Bill which unfortunately did not meet the approval of Mr. Bower, but which I did hope to submit to the approval of the House of Commons, which to my mind would have brought the railwav law into conformity with common law principles, and make the last party whose immediate negligence was the cause of the loss, the party to pay foir that loss. The exceptional circumstances that attend the operation of railways, and the exceptional advantage a railway company has over private individuals, should make it responsible for disabusing itself of that negligence and should throw upon it the burden of showing that it was not negligent. That would not be hard to do. If the company provided the best possible guard, kept its fences up and its gates 2974
(closed, it) would not be negligent, and should not be held liable. The two principles of law pertaining to railway companies should be these. They should in every case be responsible, where under common law principles an individaul would be responsible; and, by virtue of the great advantage they have over the ordinary individual whose animals are injured, they should shoulder this additional responsibility, and have the burden where in the ordinary case the plaintiff has the burden. If we embody that in the Railway Act we clearly cover the ground. But to alter section 294, which has been the foundation of all the legal decisions which have made the law pretty clear, and substitute five new exceptions, making it not only impossible to recover, but almost impossible for counsel to advise the farmer whether he has a ground for action or not, is only to make it a case of scorpions instead of whips. I submit that these amendments should not pass at the present time. If it can be shown that they in any degree relieve the difficulty under which the farmers of the west suffer to-day, I will vote for them; but I can see no advantage in them except the striking out of clause which I support. From that on they are doomed not only to produce confusion, but to make it more difficult to advise the farmer whether he is shouldering a lawsuit or the hope of success, and at the same time to make it impossible in many cases that now exist to advise him clearly that he has any case at all.

Both sides are evidently agreed as to what the law should be. The difference is only one of interpretation. Surely both parties can get together and draft a clause which will carry out the meaning of what the House wishes.
What change does the minister propose in subsection (b) ?
I was going to prefix these words:	' Other than an officer, contractor or employee of the company.'

It should be 'other person than the owner.' You are putting the liability on the farmer for the acts of somebody else. Why not say the converse of what you have-unless it is the-owner or an agent of the owner? Why should he take the risk of other people s acts? I think I made it quite distinct what the vice of this proposed legislation is. Under the present law, unless the owner or his agent or custodian is guilty of some negligence, he should not be debarred from the right to recover.

If you look at the old section, you will find it provides: that no person whose animals are killed by

any train shall have a right of action if they were killed by reason of any one, for whose use any farm crossing is furnished, failing to keep the gate on such railway crossing closed.

The minister now suggests that this clause be modified so that the person shall be an officer or agent or the company. But an officer or agent of the company is not at all likely to'let an animal through. The most likely person is the mischievous or careless one who does not own the animal and is not responsible -the tramp or meddler, or trespasser. Surely the owner should have the right to recover unless he himself or some one employed by him is to blame. Subsection 4 of section 294, which we are repealing, has this declaration:
Unless the company establishes that such an animal got out through the negligence or wilful act or omission of the owner of the animal or his agent or custodian.
Why not put in these words? You are taking away the only protection the farmer has.

I notice that in the old Act the clause that corresponds to section (a) has these words:
The person for whose use any farm crossing is furnished failing to keep the gate closed.
The company is liable unless it shows that the accident was due to the person for [DOT]whose use the farm crossing was furnished, failing to keep the gate closed. But under this amendment the company escapes having to prove that. What is the reason for the difference?

It is the specific duty of some one to keep the gate closed. That is quite different from opening a gate. To my mind it is the duty of a farmer to see that the gate is closed because the gate is his. It would be very hard to prove who left the gate open, much harder than to prove who opened it. Everybody might leave a gate open who saw it open and did not close it. My own opinion is that the man responsible for keeping the gate shut is the farmer; and if it be left open, he should see that it is *shut. But the next clause imposes a penalty on the company if any of its employees left the gate open. I am strongly of the opinion that this section, as now drafted, is a great improvement on the present statute. rfhe people who have given it the most study and are most interested are of that opinion. I,coking at the thing from a business standpoint the present law contains some paragraphs, to which my hon. friend referred, which are so obscure that they give rise to great difference of opinion as to what they really mean. At any rate the farmers in the west who have lost cattle

have not been able to get paid for them, whatever the reason may be. In discussing this question with men of some legal ability, they take the ground that we ought to wipe out all this excrescence of language and show clearly that, no matter who may be in fault, the railway company shall pay for the cattle except under certain specified exceptions. This Bill is plainer than the present Act and it leaves less room for expensive lawsuits and gives greater facility to the farmers to get paid for their cattle. However, I do not want to detain the House. If my hon. friends opposite insist, we will drop the clause for the present and take it up when we meet again and let the rest of the Bill go through

I have no doubt that if we could have a private conversation- say a committee of three or four of us-I could convince the minister of things he does not yet see. There is the common law principle of contributory negligence which we must not forget. The present law provides that it shall not be contributory negligence if an animal loose on the highway gets on the railway track. But no matter how clear the liability, if you provide that if the person injured knew the danger at the time and could have avoided it, you practically nullify the provision. We have got round that hitherto by the section I have referred to. However, I am glad this is to stand. I presume it will not be proceeded ..with until after the holiday? And it will be struck out in the meantime?
Yes.

I am not a lawyer, and I do not know what would be the effect of the clause proposed, but for my own part, personally, I would be prepared to accept any amendment accepted by this House, knowing that nothing could be worse than the present situation so far as our part of the country is concerned. I would accept this Bill on trial and be glad of it, for it can be no worse than what we now have. I am sorry it is to stand over, because farmers are sustaining losses every day by having their cattle killed or injured on the railways, and in no case have the railways paid damages foT the last three or four years- and they do not make pretense of paying as the law is now; they completely ignore the claim of the farmer for the loss of his cattle.
That is good for lawsuits.
People will not attempt lawsuits, because they know they cannot win. I am very scrry the House cannot agree on something in regard to this Bill.

I am free to say that, as I read this proposed section as it stands, it

does seem to me to be a great improvement from the point of view of the farmer whose cattle are killed on the railway. Personally, I think there might be some verbal alteration that would make it clearer; but I would be sorry to be responsible for creating a situation in which the Bill would be passed and this left out, for I think leaving it out would be a distinct loss to the persons who wish to invoke the benefit of the law against the railway company in these matters.

1 would suggest that the company follow the advice of my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Herron) and let the section pass. This is not as the laws of the Medes and Persians; if it is not satisfactory we can amend it. I am not a lawyer, but I am a farmer; and from a farmer's standpoint I think this is much more satisfactory than the old clause.
Is not the present law satisfactory in your part of the country?
No.
What are the objections?
I would not like to take up the time of the House at this stage explaining to my hon. friend, but if he will take dinner with me I will tell him all about it.
No, you can't do that with me.

I would suggest alterations that, I think, will bring the opposing views together. In subsection (a) I would insert the words that are in the present subsection (a), 'for whose use any farm crossing is furnished.' That would make it read that the company shall be liable save where killing or injury of cattle is caused bv any person ' for whose use any farm crossing is furnished failing to keep the gates at each side of the railway closed, .when not in use.' In subsection (e) I would insert the word ' wilfully ' before the word ' suffering.' I am inclined to the view expressed by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Clarke) that this amendment limits the defence of the company to the subsections in section 11. Prior to that, the company would have the additional defence of negligence. But these subsections in section 11 are wider than those in the old Act. The words I suggest, if added, confine the failure to keep the gate closed to the man for whose use it is furnished, and under subsection (e) it would confine the suffering of the animals to enter upon the railway to wilfully suffering them so to enter. And if similar change were made in subsection (b) as in subsection (a) would not that meet the case and improve the law? In other words, I would
insert before the word ' leaving ' in subsection (b) the words ' for whose use any farm crossing is furnished,' making the other verbal alterations that this change would necessitate.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) understand that a man can recover damages for cattle killed on the track unless he himself, and not some stranger, left the gate open?
Mr. COWAN In regard to subsection (a), yes.
That is not the law. If any person left the gate open the man could not recover. But the law should be changed in that respect.

Did the hon. gentleman say he could not recover if a tramp left the gate open?
Mr: MEIGHEN. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke, Essex) say that if a tramp left the gate open and cattle got through the farm crossing gate-
We are not speaking of the farm crossing gate.

That is under subsection (b). I should think it strange if, with these words inserted in subsection (a) the railway company could succeed without proving that the owner for whose benefit the gate was furnished had failed to keep it closed. I thin'k the extent of subsection (a) should be limited so that that failure should be confined to the owner for whose use the farm crossing was furnished.
That was the wording, but it was held that as regards a farm crossing, a layman would not understand it to be the law.

When these words are left there it seems to reverse the whole state of affairs that has existed up to the present time. It not only repeals the clauses of the old Act which fixed the onus upon the railway company, but it declares that the onus shall _be upon the other party. Let us take an illustration. Suppose a farmer finds his horse lying upon the railway track killed. He goes into the court to recover the loss sustained by him. He knows that he did not leave his gate open, and he knows that the horse has. escaped by reason of the gate being opened. He has been guilty of no wrong and his servant or workman has not been guilty of any wrong. In connection with that one must recollect that this railway has been put upon his farm against his wish or will, and that it is something he could not possibly prevent. This dangerous thing which has killed his horse has been forced upon him. He should be surrounded by every possible protection, but if this section passes, what is the result? He finds his horse dead, and he sues the railway company to recover the damages which he has sustained. When he goes into court he is met by this section, and he must prove, first, that his horse was killed by the railway. He proves the value of his horse. He has to prove that his horse was not killed by reason of any person failing to keep the gate at his farm crossing closed. He has to prove that no' person left the gate on either side of the railway open. He has to prove that no other person, other than an officer, contractor, or employee of the company took down any part of the fence. Then, he has to prove that nobody led, drove, or suffered the animal to be put upon the railway. He has to prove every one of these negative propositions, and it is utterly Amjpossible for him to prove them. He can go into court, and put his agent, his boys, and his girls, into the witness box and prove that no one of them did any of these acts, but for him to prove that no other person did them is utterly impossible, and the result will be that

unless he does prove any of these things he will be non-suited by the court. Under the old law that condition of affairs is reversed. If he finds his horse killed upon the railway track the onus is upon the railway company to prove that it got there *through his negligence or through his wilful act. This entirely reverses the whole situation. This is most dangerous legislation. It is most unfair because this dangerous thing has been placed there against the man's wish, he had no way of preventing it, and yet you make him responsible for everything that happens. It would make it reasonably fair if the onus of proof were confined to the acts of the owner, and if, instead of the words, ' any person ' it read ' or injury is caused by Teason of the act of the owner, his agent, servant, or workman.' He could prove that, but when it is left open by the use of the words ' any person,' he cannot recover at all.

better than I did. He has put it more concisely, and the Minister of Railways ought to be able to answer it. I understood the Minister of Public Works to deny that a person going into court to a statutory right has to prove the statutory exceptions to that right. I understood him to say he does not have to prove those statutory exceptions.

What I said was that the section makes the company expressly liable save in certain excepted cases. I said that my view of the law was that the company would have to prove the exceptions, and I think that is manifest from this: suppose a plaintiff went into court and proved that his animal was killed on a railway track and there was no further evidence, the judge would in that case direct the jury that the plaintiff was entitled to recover, and if the company wished to prove there were exceptions, which took his right to recover out of that express provision of the statute, the onus would be on the company to prove that.

The minister then recognizes that the right of the owner of the animal killed is a statutory right. If that be the case I say with all deference to the minister, who in times gone by was a lawyer, that it is elementary law that that man cannot come into court and assert a statutory right without proving and without having upon him the burden of proving that he comes within none of the statutory exceptions to that right. I cannot understand from what source the Minister of Public Works gathers his knowledge. I am not professing to have the most profound knowledge of all the principles of law. but I think I know whereof I speak when I say that no farmer who had a horse destroyed by a railway and who went into court under that provision would have a ghost of a chance of succeeding unless he alleged that he did not come within any of the exceptions and proved that he did not. It is an elementary principle of law that where a man has a common law right, he has to prove the facts that give him a right to recover; but in a case of a statutory "right, he has to prove that he is within the four corners of the Act; and you will find it in all the reports in every case dealing with statutory right, that he must prove that he does not come vrithin the statutory exceptions to that right. So that I can see no possible objection to the amendment suggested by the hon. member for North Grey. Every company .shall make crossings for persons across whose lands the railway is carried, convenient and proper for the crossing of the railway for farm purposes.
Section 253 provides:

Section 254 says;
The company shall erect and maintain upon the railway, fences, &c.
The amendment I propose is as follows:
In the exercise of his rights, as set forth in sections 252, 253 and 254, the claimant may apply concurrently either to the provincial *courts having jurisdiction in the matter of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and sections 252, 253 and 254 are amended accordingly.
. My reason for proposing this amendment us that the courts have construed section 253 as taking aw'ay the jurisdiction from ^he provincial courts in this matter. I rthink it is important to restore this jurisdiction. This section of the law, though It seems very clear and inoffensive, has [DOT]given rise to a great deal of contention and controversy. Twelve judges, seven in the province of Quebec and five in the Supreme Court here, have given judgment *on this question. Seven have decided on one side and five on the other side. And the result has been that the five were right against the seven. I consider that it is in the interest of the farmer not to be obliged, when he needsl a farm crossing or when he needs a fence repaired, to be obliged to come to Ottawa and make his application to the Board of Railway Commissioners. I do not believe that, at the beginning, it was the intent of parliament to create in that board a tribunal to decide points in litigation. For these reasons, I move the amendment which I have read.

The Board of Railway Commissioners was established to deal with these very matters. It is not stationary in the city of Ottawa, but traverses the entire country where business arises which de-Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
mands its attention. It gives a quick and ready adjustment of these differences. Only to-day I read in the paper of a widow woman writing a letter to the board about a railway crossing. The railway was asked if the letter were true, and when it (the railway) said, ' yes,' judgment was given, and the question settled. It would disarrange the whole machinery for the control or management of these things if we were to refer1 them to every court in every province. I think it would be reactionary legislation and not in the public interest. I would certainly ask the committee not to accept it.

I think there is something to be said

At six o'clock I was saying, in support of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel), that his proposition does not involve withdrawing jurisdiction from the Railway Commission. In all cases such as referred to by the minister, where the matter is very simple and can be disposed of by an application, which might be made by letter, the jurisdiction of the Railway Commissioners would remain perfectly untouched. In cases of that kind the parties would take their cases to the commission. But there is another class of cases, cases in which the right m*y be subject to serious dispute, and where it may be necessary for one side or the other to examine a number

of witnesses. Now, I fail to see that any injury could be done if, in cases of that kind, it were made possible for the person seeking to enforce his rights, to address himself to the ordinary tribunal. It is true that the Railway Commission moves around from place to place, but I hardly think it would be desirable that the Railway Commission should transport itself to the remotest limits of the county of Terrebonne, or the county of Gaspe or any back county, for the purpose of hearing a contested claim for a railway crossing. Yet if that were not done, you would put perhaps a large number of people, and in many cases poor people, to heavy expense as well as trouble and inconvenience, by having to go into some large centre where the commission is sitting, to be heard up^on the matter. After all, the right involved is a purely civil right, given, if you will, by a statute of this Dominion; and it is a reasonable proposition that the right should be allowed to stand, as it was certainly understood to be up to the time of the judgment of the Supreme Court, to which my hon. friend from Terrebonne referred; that is to say, in a condition where, though the Railway Commission would continue to have jurisdiction, a jurisdiction which might be very advantageously exercised in certain cases, there would still remain a jurisdiction in the ordinary tribunal of the province to deal with the matter. It is doubtful whether the statute meant to take away that jurisdiction from the ordinary civil tribunals, because the courts themselves were, as my hon. friend pointed out, divided upon the question. I can see no injury that would result, either to the railway companies or to the parties interested, from leaving it open to the complainant to address himself to the Superior Court. There are cases where justice is more satisfactorily obtained before an ordinary tribunal than before the Railway Commission. The amendment would leave the very beneficent jurisdiction of the Railway Commission still in existence, and liable to be exercised in oases to which it is appropriate.

The decisions of the Railway Board in regard to these crossings have been eminently satisfactory. The commission has all the machinery for hearing evidence, and further, they have a full engineering staff at their disposal. In a dispute as to the practicability of a crossing they despatch an engineer, no matter where it is, to make an examination on the ground and report. It seems to me the proposition before the committee is rather calculated to favour litigation. It looks to me as if it would be a breeding ground for litigation rather than >a quick and speedy way of settling disputes. '

I do not want to give too many quotations, but I want tb remind the House of one or two statements which have been made by public men upon this question. The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in 1907, speaking in the House of Commons made this statement:
We have a growing trade with Japan, _ a trade which must be improved; and which will assume in years to come, and in the very near future, very large proportions.
On December 16, 1907, the Prime Minister, speaking to a delegation from the T.rades and Labour Council, said:
The treaty has proved of great advantage, and our trade with Japan under it has considerably increased.
There have been many other statements made by supporters of the present government along similar lines. I find that the Prime Minister, speaking before the Manufacturers' Association in 1907 spoke in a similar strain upon this subject. Amongst others I have an extract here from a speech by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) delivered in this House, on December 6, 1907. That hon. gentleman said:
1 say that if the full development of British Columbia is to take place, we must have a share of oriental trade. The prosperity of that country, the development of its brade, require a market in the orient ***.*. Now, Sir, the trade with Japan, in my opinion, is tremendously important.
Then, again on January 28, 1908, the same hon. gentleman said:
The commercial * future of the Pacific coast depends very largely upon the extension of Canadian commercial markets in the Orient.
And he added:
We want the chief productions of Japan, articles that are desirable for our consumption, when those productions do not come into competition with our own productions.
A sentiment which I wish he had given utterance to in connection with the recent reciprocity negotiations. Then, we have the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) making a speech upon this subject In which he dealt with the hopeful outl.ook from his point of view with regard to certain classes of manufactured goods. In Hansard of 1905, page 7192, he is reported to have said:
There are the following manufactured goods in which Canada might reasonably expect to enter into trade with Japan: cotton goods, woollen goods, paper, enamelled kitchen goods, rubber good6, wire of all kinds, hats and cops.
I think it might be of interest to the House to have on record exactly what the state of Japanese trade with Canada has been during the past few years. I propose dealing, not with the year 1907, because that was a nine months' period and that was the first year in which the treaty was in effect. But, for purposes of comparison I propose to take three years prior to that beginning with 1904 and coming down to 1910. If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will permit me, I would very much like not to weary the House with all these figures, but to put them on ' Hansard ' assuring him they have been compiled by the statistician of the Customs Department at the commissioner's request.
