speechtext:
I would like to give just a brief analysis of these figures as bearing on the general theory of the trade question with the Orient and especially with Japan. I may say frankly that possibly the greatest benefit we have derived in Canada in so far as any preferential treatment or any benefit which we have enjoyed under our trade arrangement with the Orient has been with regard to the article of lead. We have preferential treatment on lead which amounts practically to 79 cents a ton. That is one of the larger items, the export of which amounted last year to $182,836. With the exception of lead, however, we practically find no encouragement at all.	We can point to two items,
pickled salmon and pickled herrings, which are the only items totalling over $100,000 and we do not enjoy the benefits of the conventional tariff with Japan on these items. Japan's tariff, as the House probably knows, while not very protective as it exists at present, is now being placed upon a more protective basis by the new arrangement which will become operative on July 17. With regard to these two special items affecting the trade of British Columbia, there is no material advantage as far as Canada is concerned for the simple reason that practically all of that particular industry is in the hands of the Japanese who are resident in British Columbia. They practically carry on the whole of that business, it enures only to their advantage, and they ship these goods to their own people.
Then, I take up the next item with regard to which a great many hopes were raised in the minds of people, not only in the east, but especially in the west. I refer to the question of lumber. We find that in the three years subsequent to the treaty we have actually exported less lumber than we exported in the three years prior to the treaty, showing that, in so far as the benefits that are derived from the treaty go, we have not received any great amount of advantage. The encouragement of trade with Australia and Bouth Africa would be far more valuable in the development of our western lumber trade. There
are a good many reasons which we never expect any very great advances in the development of our timber trade with Japan. There is the protective tariff that exists in some lines by reason of which we cannot hope to derive much advantage, and there is also, what the House may not know, that sixty per cent of the total area of Japan is covered with a carefully preserved forest. All of these 58,000,000 acres are directly under government supervision. So large is this industry in Japan itself that the dues to the government for cutting timber amounted in 1907 to no less than 12,000,000 yen, that is $6,000,000. In 1908, Japan exported $4,500,000 worth of various timber products and imported only $700,000 worth, so that, on the whole, I do not think there is any very great expectation of a big trade being built up along those lines.
I might deal somewhat hurriedly with other productions on which large hopes of Oriental trade were based in this country. One has first to observe that nearly all the agricultural products of Canada are protected in Japan, and in the new Japanese tariff there is a tendency to a higher rate of protection on practically all the various agricultural lines; in very few of them, with the exception of condensed milk which has a conventional tariff that gives us a slight advantage, have we any preference in the markets of Japan; she does not place any of these things on the *conventional tariff. Take cheese and butter, hams and bacon, vegetables and fruits, not only do we get no preference in the markets of Japan, but in every one of these articles the tariff which goes into operation on July 17 is actually higher than the tariff that has been in existence in the last few years.
I come now more particularly to the wheat question, because great expectations were based on the development of the trade in wheat, and flour from Canada to the Orient. We have heard a great many extravagant statements from all sources as to the enormous trade and the enormous advantage to Canada to be reaped from the development of our wheat and flour trade with Japan. I need only say that our expectations have not been realized. Our actual exports have been insignificant. In 1904, we shipped $602 worth of wheat to Japan, and we have not shipped any in any other year except 1907 when we shipped $1,525 worth. We are told that Japan is a very large consuming country with a population of 52,000,000 _ in an area not much greater than the riding I have the honour to represent. Being such a congested population we have been led to suppose by some of our free trade friends that naturally they would welcome free all the products that went to supply food to their people. Curiously enough.

under the present tariff we have to pay a duty of 57 sen a hundred kin. A sen is half a cent, which makes 28i cents on 132 pounds or 12i cents a bushel. I am advised that under their new tariff they have actually raised that tariff, not very much, but from 5 sen to 60 sen per 132 pounds, nor do we get the preference. The average production of wheat in Japan, for Japan is a wheat growing country, to some extent, as reckoned by Mr. Crowe, the Commercial Attache of Great Britain in Japan, for the seven years ending in 1908, is placed at 19,500,000 bushels and as Japan is very largely a rice eating population it is not at all likely that over and above their own supply they will ever very largely increase their imports. Another element is that they are developing their wheat raising areas in their northern country, in the Hokkaido district and in the future there will be a tremendous development of one of the biggest wheat growing areas in the world, in Manchuria.
The greatest hopes of trade were built on flour. In the three years subsequent to the passage of the treaty ratified by this parliament in 1907, we actually exported less flour to Japan than we did in the three years before the ratification of that treaty. Flour is again a protected item in Japan. Under the present tariff there is a considerable duty, and we get no preference under the conventional tariff now or under the new arrangement. The present tariff on flour is 1 yen, 45 sen per 100 kin, or 72i cents per 132 pounds. In the new tariff they propose to raise that to 1 yen, 65 sen per 100 kin or 82J cents per 132 pounds, which is rather a heavy protection on flour. As a matter of fact, from 1898 to 1908 the figures as they apply to the importation of flour into Japan are the reverse of encouraging. The imports rose to the very highest point in 1903 when there was an importation into Japan of 5,162,000 worth of flour. Since that, it has steadily sunk, and in 1908, the last year of which I have the record, it had sunk to $1,414,000. In reference to this special question of flour I would like to refer you to the experience, and to the very emphatic declarations of a man who, perhaps, has more authority to speak on this subject than any other man in America, Mr. J. J. Hill. Mr. Hill, who is a man of very large vision, a man who is reaching out to develop not only the trade of his railways, but in a large way to develop the trade of the whole country, some years ago conceived the idea that the Asiatic trade in general would be of immensely greater value to the United States^ if it was properly looked after, and for this purpose he built two of the largest shins ever put on the Pacific, the ' Minnesota ' and the ' Dakota,' of 28,000 tons each, Mr. BURRELL
to handle the traffic which he confidently expected to develop from the great central and western states when he had assisted in building up the trade with Japan. The whole story of that development is almost a romance, a romance that had rather an unfortunate ending in some ways. Mr. Hill, when he first started on the development of this trade, especially of the flour trade, made this remark. He realized that:
The country had to give to the Japanese and Chinese, wheat flour so cheap that they would use it instead of rice. Profits would have to be cut to the bone.
I do not want to go into the story of Mr. Hill's failure; it was partly owing, as a good many of us know, to the interference of the Interstate Commerce Board on the long haul rate which made it impossible for him to lay the goods down in Japan where he would meet the world's competition at a price which would meet the prices of countries producing even more cheaply than the United States. Mr. Hill remarked that whereas by 1904 the export of flour from the United Stales to Asia had increased very much, yet in 1908 it had sunk down to very much smaller figures. Another vital factor which Mr. Hill pointed out, which has to be borne carefully in mind, and which is no doubt appreciated by the government in regard to this Oriental trade, is the extraordinary difficulties and differences in the money exchanges of the two countries. Writing in 1910 Mr. Hill said this:
For the present we can sell some flour in China and Japan, until the Manchuria uplands shall be turned into wheat fileds. Then China can grow wheat at a cost of seventy cents a bushel in silver, which is about equal to thirty cents in gold in this country.
I do not know that I need say any more about the flour and wheat question. I would like now to refer briefly to a larger phase of trade namely, that relating to manufacturing industries. I have already referred to the statement of the Minister of Agriculture about the hope he had of our building up a trade in manufactured cotton goods, hats, caps, and articles of that kind. I mi.ght point out that even with the British preference lowering the general rate of our duties on these things, we still have on these articles for the benefit of the Canadian manufacturer, a duty of from 221 to 25 per cent against the British manufacturer. How we can expect to compete in these articles with the British manufacturer in the open markets of Japan on an even footing is a conundrum which I leave the Minister of Agriculture to answer; I confess I am not able to answer it. As a matter of fact, our trade with Japan in these lines, especially in cotton manufactures, is

practically a nagligiable quantity. Our exports of cotton fabrics to Japan were never heavy; they are diminishing, and last year they reached a figure of only $9,804; and I think we may fairly expect that they will go to the vanishing point in the near future. I may add that in 1908 Japan exported in cotton yarn? and cotton fabrics over $21,000,000 worth. She has steadily increased her importations of raw cotton, and has developed _her factory system in a marvellous way. The Japanese Year Book of 1910, in which hon. members will find a lot of valuable information in 'regard to Japanese development along industrial lines, states that the textile industry alone employs 354,000 employees, and that a few years ago the wages of these employees averaged 16 cents for men, Hi cents for women, and 6 cents for children, large numbers of women and children being employed. It is quite true, there has been a rise of wages in recent years, but not after all a very heavy one. In the report, Mr. Crowe, from which I have already quoted, showing the rise of wages between 1902 and 1908, placing the wages of 1902 at 100, and by 1908 they had 'risen to only 134-76, which is not a very heavy increase; nor, with Japan's conditions of population, is there likely to be a very rapid advance, at any rate such an advance, as will bring them within measure-able distance of what we have to pay on this continent. An analysis of present industrial conditions, especially in regard to manufactures, is not only discouraging, but absolutely alarming to the future trade of this country, for two reasons; and here again I will refer to a remark of the Minister of Agriculture, which will be found at page 888 of ' Hansard,' December 18, 1907:
The advantages secured in regard to Japan are of the utmost importance to our manufacturing industries.
I -must cpnfess that I cannot agree with that, and anybody who has given any close study to this subject will hardly agree with this opinion of the Minister of Agriculture. It is a subject profoundly interesting, but a detailed examination of the matter at this time would only weary the House. I will, however, quote again Mr. J. J. Hill, who has given a more comprehensive, and close study of commercial conditions in the far east than any other living man. He says:
Japan has organized her industry with the same scientific attention to details that she gave to her military operations. She has her own shipyards in which her ocean carriers are huilt. She has her own factories, in which almost every manufactured commodity obtained heretofore from Europe or the United States is made by her own artisans, working for wages that would not be accepted here. She is preparing and hoping to dominate the 298
Oriental markets, and to invade those of the rest of the world. . . The markets of Europe, our own markets, may, not long hence, be full of goods made in the Orient, for sale at prices so low that no tariff endurable by our own people would keep them out. . . The country needs to rid itself of the illusion that its Oriental trade is to be one of the big elements of its future prosperity.
To show the actual results of the industrial development of Japan, I might quote from a report prepared by the Foreign Trade Association of Japan, which says that the total volume of exports during the ten months ending last October amounted to 373,452,000 yen, the value of the yen being equal to 50 cents, the figures being an increase of 43,999,000 yen over the figures for the corresponding period of last year. The most conspicuous items of the increase were manufactured articles and manufactured raw materials, which showed a conspicuous increase of 15,429,000, and 22,595,000 yen respectively. That is enough to .show, without going more fully into the subject, that any hope that we have built on a market in Japan for our manufactures along almost any line, is entirely illusory. It has been a favourite theory of some people that not only will this trade be valuable to our manufacturers and our producers generally, but that it will cause an immense development of the Canadian merchant marine on the Pacific. My own opinion, based on the researches of a great many people who have given this matter a lot of study, is that the markets of both the United States and Canada will in the future be far more valuable to Japan than Japan's market will be to us. But with regard to shipping, the Prime Minister especially has been seized with the idea that it is going to be a great thing for^ Canada, and in Vancouver last fall, on "his western trip, he made these remarks :

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TRADE RELATIONS WITH JAPAN.

speechtext:
Now with these Japanese and Chinese we can only trade in what we produce. We can do there what has been done in our own country. We can exchange our flour for their tea; and, therefore, my fellow-citizens of Vancouver, there is a future in this Oriental trade. This city must trade with the Orient as well as with the Occident. And if I have the happiness again-as I know I have the certainty in my purpose-when I come again to Vancouver-as I hope to come again soon-because if I don't come soon I will not come at all- and, therefore, when I come soon, I hope now, and feel sure that I will see this noble harbour, second to none in the world, full of steamers plying between China, Japan, India and Canada. This is the hope that I have cherished, and I believe it is a hope that will be realized.
The Prime Minister has referred on other occasions to this Pacific Ocean trade, and has expressed extremely rosy, optimistic, and I think wholly illusory sentiments in

regard to our share of that sea-borne traffic. To those who have noted the various phases of Japan's commercial development in the last twenty years, nothing is so significant, I might almost say portentous, as the extraordinary expansion of her merchant marine. In 1884 there was not a single Japanese vessel navigating any but Japanese waters. In 1890 Japan had 1,450 seagoing vessels with a tonnage of 145,000. In 1900 she had 4,500 vessels with a tonnage of 600,000; and in 1908, 5,654 vessels with 1,543,000 tons. One noticeable feature of this growth is the conversion of sailing vessels to steamers, and while it was thought at one time by many of our shipping people that the Japanese would never make expert sailors, so far as their officers are concerned, the facts show the contrary, because Japanese officers are practically handling the whole of this fleet. The Japanese marine will always be more cheaply paid than can possibly be the case in the United States or Canada, for the reason that Japan has a larger population to draw on, three millions of her people being engaged in the fishing industry at of course much smaller wages than we pay our fishermen. This Japanese marine has been developed for national purposes, along scientific lines, with systematic organization and precision, and has also been aided by very considerable bounties. Under her navigation and ship building encouragement laws, Japan has spent enormous sums of money. As far as I can figure it out, this year she is paying something like $4,000,000 on subsidies for ship construction and to various shipping companies.
I might give one more reference to show the ship development there has been quite recently in that country. Another very large steamship company has been organized in Japan under the name of the Nippon Yusen Kaisha Company. That company has been organized in order to be ready for the opening of the Panama canal which, it is expected, will be finished in 1915, and thus be in a position to capture a large share of the trade through that canal. A gentleman, who is largely responsible for the organization of that company, made these remarks concerning its plans:
An idea of the extent to which the trade of Japanese shipping companies has grown is given in the address made by R. Kondo, president of the Nippon Yusen Kaisha, at the banquet held on December 15 at Tokio to commemorate the twenty-fifth anniversary of the company. He said that the N. Y. K. which started this trans-Pacific line in 1900 has reached the sixth place in order of the world's shipping companies. It has now a fleet which aggregates 280,000 tons and includes six vessels of 8,600 tons each. Prom the point of view of a commercial carrying agent it is noteworthy that whereas the foreign trade of Japan in 1805, the year before the company open-Mr. BURRELL
ed it s first regular ocean-going lines, aggregated $129,000,000, and the share carried by Japanese steamers amounted to only 3 per cent -the foreign trade in 1009 totalled some $403,000,000, no less than 45 per cent of which was carried by Japanese steamers.
These figures indicate fairly the general trade situation, as it exists between us and Japan and is likely to exist in the future. In apologizing to the House for dealing with this trade question at such length, I venture to think there is some justification for my doing so because in the earlier days I find, throughout the various negotiations such as these which the minister proposes to bring down, it was generally assumed that the commercial advantages would be so great as to justify concessions in more important directions. But the fundamental fact, the vital feature of the whole oriental question, from the point of view of any man who has made a study of it, especially from the western point of view, is the oriental immigration and the danger of such an immigration in large quantities to the vast unfilled spaces of our great west, notably British Columbia.
With regard to the resolution before the House, with regard to the arrangement to give us favoured-nation treatment in the markets of Japan, I do not want to be understood as opposing any arrangement that will put us on an equally favourable footing in the Japanese market as the United States; but I think I have shown that the conditions are such that the hopes of any great commercial prosperity arising from * treaty with Japan, are wholly illusory. Therefore, the paramount, almost the sole reasons, which should guide us in any trade arrangement with Japan are those which concern the question of immigration, which is really the strictly national and vital feature of the whole thing. I understand from the return that the government proposes to enter into direct treaty arrangement with Japan. While it is true that the British treaty, as is stated in the correspondence brought down, may not be altogether adapted to the commercial situation in Canada, it might be well to point out that in adhering to any treaty with Great Britain, we would have all the weight and authority of the empire at our back. Whereas in making a treaty direct we would be without that tremendous prestige, that great reserve power which is expressed in that simple phrase ' British power.'
The United States treaty with Japan, which has recently been ratified, has two very important safeguards, certainly more real and essential than the shadowy one we have had in past treaties. Our treaty, I understand, will expire on July 17, next, and we then resume that control which is the inalienable right of every nation-the control over immigration. I do not know

that I can do better than quote in justification of that absolute control, the citation read by the Minister of Public Works, publicly the other night from Chief Justice Marshall. Speaking of the principles of international law underlying all these questions, he said:
The jurisdiction of the nation within its own territory is necessarily exclusive and absolute. lit is susceptible of no limitation not imposed by itself. Any restriction upon it, deriving validity from an external source, would imply a diminution of its sovereignty to the extent of the restriction, and an investment of that sovereignty to the same extent in that power which could impose suoh restrictions. All exceptions, therefore, to the full and complete power of a nation within its own territories must be traced up to the consent of the nation itself. They can flow from no Other legitimate source.
I can only say in closing that if this arrangement were to diminish at all that control which we should have at the expiration of the treaty, it will be the right time for us to again reassert the supreme necessity of our having that control within our own territory. And if that question does develop in the course of the discussion in committee, I shall hope to have an opportunity of touching upon it as well.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TRADE RELATIONS WITH JAPAN.
speechtext:
The relations between Japan and Canada have been governed for some years by a treaty which will expire on the 17th of July next. The foundation of that arrangement is to be seen in a treaty made between Great Britain and Japan on the 16th of July, 1894. The treaty did not immediately apply to Canada. It contained a proviso that the self-governing Dominions, as we usually described the larger colonies, should be excepted from the operation of the treaty, but that they might be brought within its operation by special arrangement. Canada, therefore, had the opportunity to adhere to that treaty but did not at the time, or for some years, avail herself of that opportunity. I do not think we suffered any serious disadvantage from non-adherence to the treaty in any respect save one. We did find some embarrassment as affects customs tariffs. We found that other countries were having advantages in Japan which Canada did not enjoy, and naturally that was regarded with anxiety by parties in lines of trade in which it was hoped for an extension of business with Japan. For that reason largely, I think, it was determined to open negotiations, and, in 1906, a supplementary treaty was made under which the British treaty (to which I have already referred was applied to Canada. From, that day until the pre-298i
sent time we have been under the operation of that treaty.
Treaties of that character are very .broad and comprehensive and elaborate in their terms. To the ordinary layman who reads them it would probably seem that there is much repetition in them. But there is no dou'bt that all that is in them is put there for a good purpose. As we read the treaty it deals with travel and residence; protection of person and property; free and easy access to the courts; right to employ counsel; conditions with regard to freedom of worship; exemption from compulsory military or naval service; reciprocal freedom of navigation in a general way; protection of dwellings, factories, &c. Article 5, of which I make special mention because it is the subject of our present measure, provided that no higher or other duties could be imposed on the products of Japan on the one side or of Canada on the other, than are imposed upon like products of most favoured nations. Article 6 deals with equality of duties as to exports. Proceeding with the various articles we find in various matters of trade and commerce equality of treatment is stipulated. British vessels and Japanese vessels were to have equal treatment in various shipping matters; equal privileges in unloading; coasting trade excepted; equal privileges of vessels in distress; privileges of consuls to the respective countries; equality in all matters of commerce and navigation; protection of trade marks or patents; conditions with respect to foreign settlement in Japan; and certain Qther things, all no doubt necessary in a treaty of this character, but most of them things which a country like Canada would grant to any other country without any treaty stipulations. While it might be well that we should have undoubtedly the right to protect ourselves in all these things, yet, as a matter of fact, in all these things Canada would be disposed to .grant to any country equality of treatment. But we found, as I have stated, that in the absence of any commercial arrangement we were at a disadvantage owing to the lack of a treaty, and for that reason largely steps were taken in 1906 to bring Canada within the operation of the British treaty of 1894. That treaty has been in operation, as I have said, until this time. Japan, not long ago, determined to put an end to her commercial treaties and leave herself free to make a fresh start. In consequence of this general policy, notice was given to the British government that the British treaty would fall on the 17th of July next, and with it would also fall the special treaty relating to Canada. So, on that date, as matters stand, we shall cease to have any treaty obligation with Japan. The British government have

recently made a new treaty with Japan, not very materially differing from the old treaty. As usual, we have the opportunity to adhere to that treaty. But we thought it best that we should not do so. Recently, the Japanese authorities, through their Consul General at Ottawa, approached us, and rather urged that we should adhere to the British treaty as the best way of continuing friendly relations with Japan. But, upon close examination of the British treaty we thought it not particularly adapted to Canada, and, on the whole, prefer to have further time for consideration. And so it has been suggested that we should make a temporary arrangement on the only point which seems of immediate importance, and that is in relation to the customs tariffs of the two countries. It is true, as the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) has pointed out, the trade with Japan is not so extensive as we could desire. Our exports have not been increasing in the way we at one time hbped. But we all agree that, though the trade is not all that we could desire we do not want to diminish it or to find ourselves at a commercial disadvantage in Japan, compared .with other countries. We have suggested to the Japanese authorities, leaving all the other matters in the old treaty 'to be dealt with by the mutual goodwill of the two countries, that we should make a temporary arrangement with them confined entirely to the various matters in article 5 of the old treaty. Let me .read article 5 to show exactly what we are now proposing to do:
No other or higher duties shall be imposed on the importation into the dominions and possessions of Her Britannic Majesty of any articles, the produce or manufacture of the dominions and possessions of His Majesty the Emperor of Japan, from whatever place arriving; and no other or higher duties shall be imposed on the importation into the dominions and possessions of His Majesty the Emperor of Japan of any article, the produce or manufacture of the dominions and possessions of Her Britannic Majesty, from whatever place arriving, than on the like article produced or manufactured in any other foreign country; nor shall any prohibition be maintained or imposed on the importation of any article, the produce or manufacture of the dominions and possessions of either of the high contracting parties, into the dominions and possessions of the other, from whatever place arriving, which shall not equally extend to the importation of the like article being the produce or manufacture of any other country. The last provision is not applicable to the sanitary and other prohibitions occasioned by the necessity of protecting the safety of persons, or of cattle, or of plants useful to agriculture.
We have proposed, therefore, that we shall extend to Japan for- a period not greater than two years the provisions in Mr. FIELDING
effect of that article; that is to say, while we should have no special rates of customs duties between the two countries, each guarantees to the other that it will grant what is called ' most favoured nation treatment/ that is: We shall grant to Japan no less favourable treatment than we grant to any other foreign country. Of course, the term ' foreign country ' is used for a purpose, because it does not interfere with our liberty to make any arrangement that we deem proper within the British Empire. But if we adopt this arrangement, for a period not exceeding two years, practically the same conditions we now grant to other foreign countries we will grant to Japan. We have received information from the Japanese authorities that regarding this as a temporary arrangement, they will be content to meet the suggestions we have offered. Some correspondence has been brought down, only one or two letters of which I think have any immediate bearing on the proposed arrangement; and with your permission I will read these, because they will give in brief space the nature of the arrangement we propose to make. This letter is dated the 10th of May, and is addressed by myself to the Consul General for Japan residing in Ottawa:
Ottawa, May 10, 1911.
Sir,-Referring to our several interview!] and to the note veribale of the 24th April last, communicated to me by you this day in an amended form, I have to obsetrve that the terms and conditions of the treaty of the 3rd April, 1911, between Great Britain and Japan do not seem to be in tbeir entirety adapted to the circumstances of Canada, and, therefore, we have some hesitation in advising that immediate adherence to it on the part of Canada which your government desires.
Article 8 of the treaty of the 3rd April provides that:
'The articles, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom, enumerated in Part I of the Schedule annexed to this treaty, shall not, on importation into Japan, be subjected to higher customs duties than those specified in the Schedule.
'The articles, the produce or manufacture of Japan, enumerated in Part II of the Schedule annexed to this treaty, shall he free of duty on hnportation into the United Kingdom.'
There might be a question whether in the event o f Canada giving adherence to the treaty, the schedule referred to in article 8 would thereupon become applicable to Canada. Granting, however, that it would so apply, an examination of its details shows that while no doubt well adapted to the conditions of the trade between Great Britain and Japan, the schedule is not wholly suitable to the commercial interchanges between Japan and Canada. Paid I of the Sohedule, for example, which contains a list of British products upon which maximum duties are fixed does not include many products in the export of which Canada is largely interested; and od the other

hand, Part II of the Schedule, containing a list of Japanese products to which Great Britain agrees to give admission free of duty, includes silks and other articles wibich are dutiable on importation into Canada although free of customs duty in Great Britain.

Ottawa, May 15, 1911.
Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 10th instant, setting forth the views of your government in regard to some hesitation which they have in advising immediate adherence on the part of Canada to the treaty of the 3rd April, 1911, between Great Britain and Japan, and suggesting that, leaving all other matters affecting the intercourse between Canada and Japan to the mutual good will of the two countries and the comity of nations, a temporary arrangement be made providing that from and after the 17th day of July, 1911, Canada shall receive in Japan the tariff treatment as expressed in article V of the treaty of commerce and navigation between Great Britain and Japan signed at London on the 16th July, 1894, which was made applicable to Canada by the convention between the United Kingdom and Japan respecting commercial relations between Canada and Japan signed at Tokio on the 31st January, 1906, and that reciprocally Japan shall receive in Canada the tariff treatment as expressed in the said article V.
In reply, I have the honour, duly authorized by my government, to state that the Imperial Japanese government fully concurs in the proposal therein made by you in regard to a temporary tariff arrangement engaging the reciprocal grant of the most favoured nation treatment.
I have honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) T. NAKAMURA. Consul General of Japan. The Honourable W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
It will be observed that in the communication which I sent to the consul general I confined myself to two points: First, entirely to the question of the customs tariff, all other things are allowed to stand aside, and the treaty as respects these other things will lapse. My proposal was that we Siould reciprocally have what is called the most favoured nation treatment, so-that we might guard against any other country getting terms with Japan which would place us at a disadvantage. That they have agreed to give us. Then I went on to speak of the question on which my hon. friend from Yale-Oariboo (Mr. Burrell) addressed the House, and which is one of great importance. Let me again read the paragraph on the question of immigration:

The question of immigration has been discussed between us on several occasions. I do not deem it necessary that this should be more than mentioned here, inasmuch as the assurance received from you of the willingness of your government to continue the friendly understanding on that matter at present existing, is entirely satisfactory to us.	i
Now it is necessary to observe that whatever has been done in the matter of immigration has not been done by treaty at all. Under the terms of the treaty which is soon to expire, Japanese subjects had the right to enter, to reside, to travel, and to have all the rights of British subjects in Canada. But we know that embarrassments arose from the free exercise of the rights so granted, and a friendly arrangement was made several years ago by which the Japanese government, though not going into details, not being content that the matter should be discussed very much in detail, gave this government an assurance, through the proper official of the Japanese government, to my hon. colleague the Postmaster General who was at the time in Japan, that the Japanese government would itself place certain limitations and restrictions upon immigration from Japan; and we had every reason to believe that, with the arrangement which the Japanese government, for its own purposes, was ready to make, there would be an absence of the difficulties which had unhappily arisen on our Pacific coast. That assurance so given has been fully lived up to. It is fair to the Japanese government to say that though it was never a matter of treaty, but a somewhat loose understanding, it has been acted up to in all good faith, and the number of Japanese who have desired to come into Canada has not been large. The number has been in the last year some 400, while in the last three years some 1,200 have come in. So, having received the assurance at that time that the Japanese government were prepared to deal with the problem in that way, and having received the assurance that they would continue that friendly arrangement, we have accepted that assurance and we feel that all will 'he well.
„We do not, in the resolution before the House, touch the question of immigration *at all. The old treaty undoubtedly did 'touch the question of immigration, because *if its terms had been enforced by the Japanese, it would have given them all the rights and privileges of British subjects in the Dominion; but, as I pointed out, they did not insist upon the 'exercise of the rights that came to them under the treaty. But when, on the 17th July, that treaty expires, there will be no arrangement of any kind, by law, or statute, or treaty, of a legal and
Mr. FIELDING
binding character with respect to immigration from Japan. While we would be free as a matter of law to make our arrangements with Japan in the same manner as we would be with any other country having no treaty obligations, and while we would be, under the terms, absolutely free to apply all our immigration laws and every other law to our relations with Japan, we do not hesitate to say that it is our desire and inclination to maintain that friendly understanding that already exists. We are happy to acknowledge the fact that the Japanese government have dealt with the matter in a good spirit, and we have every assurance that they mean to continue to deal with it in the same	spirit; so
that we feel that there is no probability	of	a revival	of those
unpleasant incidents that occurred on the Pacific coast several years ago. With these few explanations, I beg to ask the committee to adopt this resolution and, upon its adoption, I will have the honour to present a Bill to carry it into effect.	.

speechtext:
Before the resolution is adopted, I would like to have a little clearer understanding with respect to the matter which has been alluded to by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in his concluding remarks. I must confess that the situation does not seem to me quite so clear as it seems to him. In article 1 of the treaty of commerce, by which Canada became bound by the convention of the 31st January, 1906, it was provided as follows:
The subjects of each of the two high contracting parties shall have full liberty to enter, travel or reside in any part of the dominions and possessions of the other contracting party, and shall enjoy full and perfect protection for their persons and property.
That gave to the citizens of Japan the absolute right to enter and reside in any part of Canada. It is unnecessary to recite the troubles that arose afterwards in British Columbia in consequence of which my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) made a visit to J apan and entered upon some negotiations with the government of that country, through the intervention of the British ambassador. The result of those negotiations was embodied in a letter bearing date Tokio, December 23, 1907, addressed to the Postmaster General. That letter is in the following terms:
Monsieur le Ministre,-
In reply to your note of even date, I have the honour to state that although the existing treaty between Japan and Canada absolutely guarantees to Japanese subjects full liberty to enter, travel and reside in any part of the Dominion of Canada, yet it is not the invention of the imperial government to insist icon the complete enjoyment of the rights and privileges guaranteed by . those stipulations

when that would involve disregard of special conditions which may prevail in Canada from time to time.
Acting in this spirit and having particular regard to circumstances of recent occurrenec in British Columbia, the imperial government have decided to take efficient means to restrict emigration to Canada. In carrying out this purpose, the imperial government, in pursuance of the policy above stated, will give careful consideration to local conditions prevailing in Canada, with a view to meeting the desires of the government of the Dominion as far as compatible with the spirit of the treaty and the dignity of the state.
Although, as stated in the note under reply, it was not possible for me to acquiesce in all of the proposals made by you on behalf of the Canadian government, I trust that you will find in the statement herein made proof of the earnest desire of the imperial government to promote by every means within their power, the growth and stability of the cordial and mutually beneficial relations which exist between our countries. I venture to believe, also that this desirable result will be found to have been materially advanced by the full exchange of views which lias taken place between us, and it gives me special pleasure to acknowledge the obligation under, which I have been placed by your frank and considerate explanations regarding the attitude and wishes of your government.
I avail myself, &c., &c.,
(Sgd.) TADASTJ HAYASHI. The Honourable Bodolphe Lemieux,
Postmaster General and Minister of Labour for Canada, Tokio.
The arrangement between Canada and Japan, when that letter was written, was to be found, in the first place, in the article of the treaty which I have quoted, and, in the second place, in this letter I have just read.	The	treaty was	Ithus supplemented by an informal engagement on the part of the Japanese government that it would restrict emigration from Japan to Canada, and in doing so that it would have regard from time to time to any special conditions in Canada that made such restriction desirable in the interest of goodwill between the two countries. I am unable to divorce the letter from the article of the treaty to which that letter continually alludes. If there is no treaty there is no need of any understanding. If the continuation of the understanding means anything, it seems to me to mean the continuation of the article of the treaty to which I have just now alluded and which is almost in terms embodied in it. If you continue the understanding embodied in this letter then it seems to me you continue the article of the treaty which is not only referred to but embodied in the very letter itself.
That is one view of it. The only other view is that the treaty is absolutely gone, that the understanding is gone also, that because the treaty is gone, therefore, there is no need of any understanding and that
matters will subsist between the two countries as far as immigration is concerned, exactly as if there were no treaty. It is not the latter position which the Minister of Finance seems to take. In his letter he has, in the first place, said:
I would suggest that leaving all other matters affecting intercourse between Japan and Canada to the mutual good will of the two countries the comity of nations, a temporary arrangement be made with regard to commercial affairs.
That would be entirely consistent with the view, that, in so far as immigration is concerned, we are absolutely unhampered by any treaty or understanding, but the latter part of the letter, where special reference is made to immigration, is not consistent with that view. These are the words which have already been quoted by the Minister of Finance:
The question of immigration has been discussed between us on several occasions. I do not deem it necessary that this should be more than mentioned here, inasmuch as the assurance received from you of the willingness of your government to continue the friendly understanding bn that matter at present existing is entirely satisfactory to us.
I am unable to understand how you can continue, how it is possible to continue, that friendly understanding unless you continue as a part of that friendly understanding, because it was a part thereof, the article of the treaty of 1894 which I have quoted just now and which gives to the citizens of Japan the absolute and full right to enter and reside in Canada, subject always, of course, to the modification which is embodied in the letter written by the Japanese Minister of Foreign Affairs, to. my hon. friend the Postmaster General.

I think the error in my hon. friend's argument is in assuming that article 1 of the treaty and the arrangement respecting immigration hang together. That is the foundation of his contention. I do not think that is correct. The Japanese have always claimed that this arrangement is independent of the treaty, and I think we ought to go upon the .assumption that .that is correct. The treaty, with article 1, ceases to exist because the Japanese authorities, of their own motion, have determined that it shall cease to exist; they cannot claim that in any way that article is in operation. However, while that is_ the legal position, the technical position, I do not think it practically makes much difference, because the arrangement after all is this: We have assurances that they will themselves restrict the number of Japanese citizens coming to Canada. That is the essence of the whole. thing, they gave us that assurance several years ago,

they have lived up to it. We have the assurance. We cannot always bring down papers in relation to matters of this kind, but we have the assurance, in terms admitting of no doubt, that the Japanese authorities are willing to continue that arrangement which has worked so satisfactorily in the last three or four years. It is a point upon which the Japanese government have been rather unwilling to go into details. They have asked us to accept their assurance in good faith. We did so at the time and we have every reason to feel satisfied with the manner in which they have acted and feel that they would do the same thing in the future. We will be free, as a matter of law on July 17, from any obligation under that treaty except whatever obligation we shall assume if we adopt this resolution respecting customs tariffs; but while we will be absolutely free, as a matter of treaty and of law, to put these matters aside, we desire to give to the Japanese government the assurance that we wish to continue our friendly relations with them, and we feel that we should not take advantage of the absence of that treaty to engage, by legislation or administration, in any course of treatment different to what we apply to them to-day. If they continue, as I believe they will, in good faith to act up to that arrangement, we should be willing even without any treaty, to deal with them in a friendly spirit. That is a correct statement of the situation.

T",e minister give a single reason for it. 1 do not think he can give one reason m the public interest of Canada. I do not believe he can justify before the people of Canada having entered into that secret understanding with J apan, which does not expire on the 17th of July next, when the people of Canada believed that it would expire.
The fact is that under that friendly understanding with Japan, the Japanese people have free^ right of entry and residence In Canada, and that free right is to be Mr. COWAN.
restricted only by the Japanese government. There is nothing more to it, and we are handing over for no reason which any minister or public man dare state publicly, and are continuing to hand over, in spite of the expiration of this treaty, this power to regulate immigration into Canada. What reason can any public man give for handing over to a foreign power the jurisdiction which was given by the Act of confederation to this parliament with regard to immigration? What reason can the government give in the public interest for doing it? They can give none; and mark you, the Postmaster General (Mr. Lem-ieux) sneered once, in answer to a suggestion I made, that the right of the Japanese to enter Canada under the Japanese Treaty is less encumbered by conditions than the right of an Englishman, a Scotchman, an Irishman or a Frenchman under our Immigration Act. Perhaps the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) will make bold to say again that I am wrong in my construction of the Japanese Treaty or of the friendly understanding or of the Immigration Act. I say again you are not, by this friendly understanding, putting the immigrants from the mother land on an even keel with the immigrants from Japan; you are discriminating in favour of Japanese immigration. You cannot cut down those rights acquired by agreement between two nations hy an Immigration Act. The United States evidently believe that cannot be done because they made an express stipulation in their treaty that Japan shall be subject to the immigration laws of the United States. But under this friendly understanding which this government has entered into, every Japanese subject has an absolute right to free entry and residence in Canada except when that right is restricted by his own government. That understanding gives privileges and preference to the Japanese immigrant which the immigrants from other countries do not enjoy. Can any reason in the public interest be advanced for this discrimination in favour of the Japanese? Are we so anxious to increase the Japanese population of Canada that we are going to discriminate in their favour against Irishmen, Englishmen and Scotchmen and men from other European countries? That was the legal effect under the old treaty which expires on the 17th July next, and it will be the effect of the continued understanding between the two nations. The difference between a treaty and an understanding is the difference between tweedle dum and tweedle dee. It is infinitesimal. It does not modify the fact that when an agreement between nations is entered into, neither one has any right to pare down that agreement, and limit by legislation the rights of the citizens of the other coun-

try with regard to immigration or any other subject. So that we are presenting to the world this spectacle. We started out with a great desire to make treaties, and we blundered into this treaty in January, 1906. The government blundered into it and tried to justify it by the misleading statement that they had an agreement with Japan limiting the number of Japanese immigrants to come from Japan into Canada. Within six months after that treaty was ratified, 8,125 Japanese immigrants had landed in the ports of Vancouver and Victoria. Then my hon. friends opposite will say: Oh, but our Postmaster General went over and made this arrangement, and the number coming into the country since has been considerably reduced. With that point I propose to deal later, but the fact remains that this agreement will continue to the Japanese people the right which the people of the United Kingdom would be delighted to enjoy, the right of free entry and free residence, the right to be restricted only by the government of the country from which the immigrant comes. Suppose that right were given to Englishmen, do you not think it would increase the number of English, Scotch and Irish immigrants? Is it any wonder that the Japanese were so alert to avail themselves of this right and Tush into Canada in such numbers?
The vice of the thing is this, and no one knows it better than the Finance Minister -I venture to say that he has wished a thousand times he had never made the fatal blunder of entering into this foolish treaty of the 31st January, 1906, the vice of the thing is this, that you have selected a people who never intend to become Canadian citizens, who are unfit to become Canadian citizens, and you are giving them a preference in our immigration field over every other people in the known world.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I see absolutely no reason why we should continue this alleged friendly understanding. The advantage of the tariff arrangement has been discussed to-night fully by my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) I think he has shown that its advantages are nil. Why should we not avail ourselves of this opportunity, when this treaty is expiring, to make no arrangement that is not to the advantage and honour of Canada? The commercial side of the treaty is of little or no benefit to Canada. The balance of trade is with Japan, and gold has to go from Canada to Japan to meet that balance. This ' friendly understanding' on the subject of immigration, I venture to say, is, in the view of ninety per cent of the people who are affected by it, a most unfriendly arrangement so far as the interests of Canada are concerned. I see no necessity for Canada making any move at the present juncture. She does not
have to adhere to that agreement. There is no breach of national honour or national etiquette in our failing to adhere to that agreement. There is no advantage in adhering to that agreement or making a new commercial arrangement. Why not, with the dignity and self-respect that becomes a nation, exercise the power given us by that Confederation Act, the power to regulate and restrict and govern immigration from any country we please according to the interests of Canada? Why do we hand that power to a foreign country? What advantage are we getting in return? How does it add to our self-respect or advance any of our interests? What end is it attaining for Canada? Why not stand exactly as we are in all treaty relations between the two countries, until we can get an arrangement that is really for the interest of the country?
Now, I know of no power possessed by the government of Canada which enables it to enter into an agreement that has never been submitted to parliament for ratification and which is described by the representative of the Japanese government in this language:
The understanding arrived at between the two governments


The Canadian and the Japanese.
-in 1908 on the subject of immigration is quite independent of the existing treaty concluded between Japan and Canada in 1906 End is not terminated on the expiration of that treaty between Japan and Canada.
I am prepared to say that the Canadian government has no power to enter into a side agreement with a nation which agreement was never submitted to parliament and is not part of the British treaty. I am prepared to state that the government does not need to take the view that there exists any understanding or agreement independent of the treaty and not expiring with the treaty. There is no necessity put upon the government to take that view; and I say it is in the interest of Canada generally that no such view should be taken, and no action taken such as the minister has outlined tonight.
I can only say, in conclusion, that I know that the people who live in these conditions, and who are as broad and generous-minded as any other part of the electorate of Canada, regardless of occupation or origin, race or creed, are of one mind in believing that it is a fatal mistake in the interests of Canada, looking to her larger destiny, to encourage by treaty or friendly understanding with Japan, the immigration of people who never intend to become citizens of Canada and who take the place in that western country of men wdro should be citizens undertaking the responsibilities of citizens. In that western country we have duties to perform; we have to establish

there the institutions that have made Canada and the other portions of the British Empire what they are. We have to do this by our own exertions. And when you find that of the people we are adding to the population of this country, twenty-five per cent of them at least are aliens and intend to remain aliens, who intend to leave the country, who take upon themselves no part of the duties of citizenship-I tell you that you are casting upon what the Prime Minister (iSir Wilfrid Laurier) in an unfortunate moment called the ' white portion of British Columbia.' a burden that may become,^ one of these days, greater than they can bear.
I	have no desire to refer to past events or to affect in the slightest degree the relations between Japan and Canada or between Japan and the British Empire. I hope these relations may always remain cordial. But I do say that the men who propose these arrangements with Japan on a subject which, under the Confederation Act we have the power to deal with, are not rising to the great height of Canada's destiny in those matters that affect not only Canada but the whole Anglo-Saxon race. I say there are other duties cast upon us besides this twopenny half-penny chasing after the dollar in the remote corners of the earth. I say that our patriotism should not be of that sordid kind which is measured by the price of a ton of lead in Japan or of a sack of potatoes on the Boston market. I think we have other and higher duties to perform. I feel_ that this government is failing, and failing absolutely, in the performance of those high duties, in this attempt to put through this arrangement with Japan.

speechtext:
At this late hour of the night and at this late stage of the session, I would not like to detain the House more than a moment or two. But I feel, after listening
II	the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) that I would be doing an injustice to those whom I more particularly represent in this House, the working classes of this country, if I allowed his remarks to pass without comment.
I was particularly struck with one phrase the hon. member made use of, that there was danger of casting on British Columbia a burden greater than she could bear. As I listened to his remarks I could not help feeling that if many speeches of that kind were delivered throughout Canada, we would be casting upon this country a greater burden than the people would be able to bear. I wonder if the hon. member realizes the extent and magnitude of this question of Oriental immigration. It has been my privilege to see something of the 300 millions of India, to see something of the 400 millions of China, to see something of the 50 millions of Japan; and as I wandered through those countries and Mr. COWANr
saw those multitudes, and thought that we on this side of the Pacific were a people of only 8 or 9 millions, I eould not help feeling that the manner of dealing with the problem of Oriental immigration was one of the most important and far reaching concerns of this nation. Now what is the manner my hon. frined suggests tonight? It is that we should claim the rights which we have under the British North America Act, and begin to legislate in this parliament by a series of acts in the nature of exclusion.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TRADE RELATIONS WITH JAPAN.
subtopic: IMPERIAL CONSULATE GENERAL OF JAPAN FOR THE DOMINION OF CANADA.
speechtext:
I am prepared to accept what my hon. friend says as to his statement, but every hon. gentleman in this House will draw his own inference from his remarks. There are only two methods by which this question of Oriental immigration can be dealt with. There is either the method of diplomacy which this government has followed, and there is the other method of hurling defiance in the face of these Oriental people and telling them that, despite their numbers, despite their industrial and commercial importance, we shall legislate against them in a fashion which will exclude them totally from our shores. Now I believe with all my heart that it is absolutely necessary to restrict immigration from the Orient. I think in the interest, not only of the working classes of this country, but of all other classes it is absolutely necessary that the people of the Orient shall be restrained from coming to this country. But there are two methods of doing that. One method is to attempt it by legislation, with the possibility of incurring the hostility of those peoples, the other method is to allow those people themselves to show their desire to deal with us as a friendly nation, and when they express a willingness to restrict their own emigration, if they carry out that promise faithfully, to give them an opportunity to do so, and to continue that arrangement with them as long as we have reason to believe in their good faith. Now that is the position we are in with regard to Japan at the present day.
Our position, and the posftion of the nation to the south of us, is precisely analogous in more than one particular. We have

each had a (treaty recently with Japan, a trade treaty which deals also with the subject of immigration. In the treaty with the United States I believe the American government reserved to itself the right to handle the question of immigration as it pleased. At the time we were discussing this treaty with Japan some years ago, hon. gentlemen opposite urged that we on this side of the House should have put into our agreement the same clause which was in the agreement of the United States, namely, that nothing in that trade treaty should in any way restrict our privileges in the matter of legislating on the subject of immigration. But what has taken place in the United States within the last six months as a result of their experience? The United States has entered into a new treaty with Japan, and what is the first clause in that treaty? This treaty has been signed within the past few weeks, on the fifth day of April in fact, and the first article in that treaty reads as follows:
Tlie citizens or subjects of each of the high contracting parties shall have liberty to enter, travel and reside in the territories of the other, to carry on trade wholesale and retail, to own or lease and occupy houses, manufactures, warehouses and shops, to employ agents of their choice, to lease land for residential and commercial purposes, and generally to do anything incident to or necessary for trade upon the same terms as native citizens or subjects, submitting themselves to the laws and regulations there established.

Washington. And what are the words of this declaration?
In proceeding this day to the signature of the treaty of commerce and navigation between Japan and the United States, the undersigned, Japanese ambassador in Washington, duly authorized by his government, has the honour to declare that the Imperial Japanese government are fully prepared to maintain with equal effectiveness the limitation and control which they have for the past three years exercised in regulation of the immigration of labourers to the United States.

Atlantic or on the Pacific, and the stipulation to which my hon. friend has just referred applies exactly in the same way to Canada.

I inform him that I have seen myself the officials of this government putting those laws into force on the Pacific coast, turning back men and, refusing them the right to land in this country because they were not able to pass the medical examination which was required of them. My hon. friend knows the law has been enforced out in British Columbia.

I was just going to point out to my hon. friend that under the treaty the United States have found it desirable to make with the Japanese government they have given the Japanese the free right of entry into the United States. The immigration of Japanese into the United States is restricted only by the general application of the United Slates immigration laws along lines exactly parallel to our own; that is with reference to the question of diseased and undesirable immigrants and the like. With that exception the whole matter of immigration from Japan to the United States is 'based on the declaration that:
The Imperial Japanese government are fully prepared to maintain with equal effectiveness the limitation and control which they have for the past three years exercised in regulation of the emigration of labourers to the United States.
I may say to my hon. friend that perhaps he is not aware of the fact that the agreement between Japan and the United States went into effect subsequent to the time at which the arrangement was effected between Canada and Japan. My hon. friend the Postmaster General left this Mr. KING.
country for Japan in December, 1907. He was able at that time, through negotiations with the Japanese government and with the assistance of the British Ambassador, to make an arrangement which has effectively stopped emigration of any extent from Japan to Canada. After that arrangement had been effected the United States government sought to make a similar arrangement with the government of Japan. They were successful in getting either in part or in whole what this government got with Japan, but not more; and that arrangement has been found to work so satisfactorily that the United States government, in consenting to this treaty with Japan, has accepted the assurance that this arrangement will continue to work satisfactorily as far as immigration is concerned. That assurance is given irrespective of the treaty one way or the other. It is because of the policy of the Japanese government, that they have given this assurance to two different countries. It is part of their present policy that their people shall not come to this side of the water, but that those who leave Tokio and other Japanese cities shall emigrate to different parts of the Orient, Corea and Manchuria in particular. That is why this government has found a more effective way of dealing with this question by friendly negotiations through the channels of diplomacy rather than by an attitude of defiance and by the passing of exclusion laws against the citizens of 'that country. I have some figures here which show the immigration from Japan under this present arrangement.

and that is that that arrangement was not what the Postmaster General asked when he went there; he certainly wanted something more than that, but he did not get all he asked for. I understand the imperial government is not able to accede to my wishes in the matter of limiting the number of the above immigrants. What he asked for I do not know, but he evidently thought he should get much more than he did get; at any rate he asked for it, and did not get it. The people of British Columbia are not satisfied, and have not been satisfied with this agreement as it stands. They are not satisfied because the control of this immigration is in the hands of the Japanese government to deal with as they see fit. The letter of December 23rd, 1907, which is the basis of the agreement, provides that the Japanese government is to give careful consideration to local conditions prevailing in Canada, and that for the purpose of this discussion means in British Columbia, with a view of meeting the desires of the government of the Dominion of Canada, as far as compatible with the spirit of the treaty, and the dignity of the State. speechtext: The government at Ottawa have not appreciated the feelings of the people of British Columbia, they never have from the time that this question first became a live issue. I do not wish to enter on anything particularly controversial in .connection with this matter to-night, but we have had statements from different ministers which go to show beyond question that the sympathies, and the feelings of the government were not at one with the people of British Columbia. The government undoubtedly made a blunder when they first entered into this treaty, a blunder which -was absolutely unnecessary because the details were called to their attention by the imperial government at the time, and the imperial government informed this government . that they did not need to adhere to that treaty so far as the question of immigration of labour was concerned. In spite of that they adhered to the treaty, and found themselves in trouble by reason of having, done so. At this time it would be a mistake on the part of the government to perpetuate that blunder; let this matter drop, and begin all over again. The people of British Columbia wish to develop their own province along their own lines. We think, rightly or wrongly, that we have the finest province in the Dominion. We have any amount of difficulties to overcome, and we do not want these difficulties increased by a large influx of alien population which can never be assimilated with ithe population of the province, and which will be for all time to come a detriment to it.

speechtext:
I would like to add a word or two of protest in regard to the resolution. If the resolution ps it is on the Order Paper was all that we had in connection with the matter to be dealt with,
I would have nothing whatever to say, but yesterday the Finance Minister brought

down a return of correspondence leading *up to the resolution that we have on the Order Paper. In that return I find a letter which the Finance Minister lias read' in the House this evening. In it he referred to the fact that he trusts the same relations will continue in regard to immigration that have been in existence since the letters referred to between the Postmaster General and the Imperial Japanese government were exchanged. I absolutely agree with the argument advanced by the leader of the opposition, that we must read the reference in the letter addressed by the Finance Minister to the Imperial Japanese government in connection with article 1 of the original treaty to which undoubtedly it refers.
The whole argument of the lion. Minister of Labour has been that they have no treaty now, and that therefore we can at any time restrict the immigration of Japanese subjects. But that is contrary to the correspondence brought down and laid on the table yesterday, and repeated by the Minister of Finance to-night. Following that argument, the Minister of Labour refers to the recent treaty between the United States and Japan, from which he endeavours to argue that they are using exactly the same agreement that we have had with the Japanese government. But what are the facts? As the hon. member for Vancouver pointed out, in the latter clause of the agreement between the United States and Japan, it is expressly stated:
And, whereas, the advice and consent of the Senate of the United States for the ratification of the said treaty as given with the un-dei-sbanding that that treaty was not to be deemed to repeal or affeot any of the provisions of the Act of Congress entitled an Act to regulate immigration into the United States.
By that clause the United States absolutely claim the right to control the immigration. The hon. Minister of Labour says that refers only to criminal immigration; but in the original treaty made with Japan that class of immigration was not excepted. That was one of the objections taken by the province of British Columbia, namely, that instead of retaining control over our own immigration, we had handed it over to the Japanese government.

speechtext: The fact that we did not expressly name our immigration Act did not exclude its provisions from applying to the Japanese in the same way as to immigration from other nations. Any labourer from Germany who could pass our laws in that regard could also come from Japan.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-TRADE RELATIONS WITH JAPAN.
subtopic: IMPERIAL CONSULATE GENERAL OF JAPAN FOR THE DOMINION OF CANADA.
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour does not seem to recognize the fact that the treaty superseded any immigration laws we had, and we had absolutely no control over either criminal or other immigration, at that time. It is quite true that possibly the Japanese government would not have taken objection	to	our	excludingcriminal immigration, although even in regard to that	we	have	no absolute right under	the	treaty	;	but we
failed to retain control over our own immigration, even of labourers from Japan. We are satisfied that this government should have friendly trade relations with Japan; but at the time this treaty was made with Great Britain, the Secretary of State for the Colonies called attention to the fact that the colonies could accept these rights and privileges with respect to trade, and yet retain control of immigration. We have no objection to trading with these people; on the contrary, we are from time to time increasing our shipping in that direction, and we desire to have trade with them; but the Japanese government, through the imperial government, said that they were quite prepared that the Dominion government should accept these trade relations and still retain control of her own immigration. What is the condition to-night? This treaty lapses in July next, and we had a right, not only as citizens of British Columbia, but as citizens of the Dominion of Canada, to expect that this government would have taken advantage of that opportunity to retain control of our own immigration. There was absolutely no necessity for the Minister of Finance, in negotiating on behalf of this government, to report that they had difficulties in regard to immigration, and practically to continue the treaty. You have not only deliberately handed over the control you had given to them by the treaty with Great Britain, but handed over that control by that letter without any reciprocal return whatever. I do not mean to say that we would value Japan as a place of immigration for Canadian citizens, but we had at least that reciprocal right by the treaty. To-day that right is taken away. The letter of the Finance Minister deals with the arrangement based on the letter about which the hon. member for Vancouver was so careful to ask, and as to which he got the assurance of both the Postmaster General and the Finance Minister



that it was the basis of the agreement. Under that letter the Japanese government indefinitely, or at least to the full extent of two years, will have the absolute right, if they so desire-and they will only be guided after an investigation of the Canadian situation-to control that immigration, and we have absolutely no rights in return.

speechtext:
And while doing that, we have not even the previous concessions, which 'we had under the treaty. There are no reciprocal concessions with regard to immigration. True there are with regard to trade, but .absolutely none with regard to immigration, and that is why I enter my protest, not only on behalf of the people of British Columbia but of the Dominion.
I do not propose at this late hour to go into all the arguments why we think this immigration is not suitable to Canada. Every one will agree that we cannot assimilate Asiatic immigration and make the Asiatics good Canadian citizens. But that is no reason why we should not trade with them, and the Japanese recognized that in the treaty of 1906 and said they were quite prepared that the Dominion should accept the advantages of a trade treaty, but still retain control of her own immigration. iNow when the opportunity arises this year tio resume our control of immigration* we find, by the letter of the Finance Minister, that the government has given away the right to control that immigration. I am free to admit, from the figures furnished by the Department of Labour which I assume are correct, that to a large extent the Japanese have restricted immigration, but that is purely a matter of goodwill on their part, and it is on that my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr, Cowan) argued that to-day the Japanese have more rights with regard to immigration than British people. They have the absolute right and freedom to come in, reside, travel, &c.-rights exceed-Mr. GOODEVE.
ing those which any other nationality has to-day. It is on that basis we object to this proposed agreement. We do not object to the proposed extension of our trade or our traffic regulations, but solely to our immigration regulations.

speechtext: If the minister's view be correct, why should the United States have found it necessary to have a special protocol making the Japanese subject to their immigration laws.

speechtext: If the clause in the United States Treaty, which says that the treaty does not exempt the Japanese from the immigration laws of the United States- and which clause is contained in the body of that treaty-has the effect my hon. friend says it has, why is it that a protocol was required outside of that treaty to continue the agreement between the United States and Japan? Why did they .want that agreement to continue if their immigration laws shut out Japanese immigration? Either one of two things. Either the United States immigration laws did not have that effect or else the United States, like ourselves, considered it better for the Japanese themselves to restrict emigration to the United States than for the Americans to pass laws and regulations to shut the Japanese .out.
