speechtext: The urgency of this item-arises from the fact that our boundary surveys are made in conjunction with those of the United States, pursuant to an understanding between the two countries that joint surveys shall be made. The survey parties have to be started out in early spring in order to do a season's work. A large part of the work is done during the summer season; a five-twelfths vote would not carry them through their summer's work and would cut them off during the summer. Part of this expenditure is for the Alaskan boundary where the work will be done this summer some distance north of the Arctic circle. In every way it is desirable that this sum should be available.
At what time does the commission complete its work for the season?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The work is always done in the summer, they come in in November.
Surveys, examination of survey returns, printing of plans, &c., $965,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The committee are aware that the township surveys of Dominion lands are carried on during the summer time. The parties have to start out early in order to do a summer's work. We have assumed that the money will be voted and the parties are now out.
How long have they been out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They started out about the first of April.
What time do they -come in?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In November. Their work is done by November. If w-e only vote five-twelfths, they will be out of money when the summer is about half through.
One would think that five-twelfths would last until we come back again?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is very expensive keeping parties in the field, and it would not be desirable to have to call them in for lack of funds.
Do they go out and remain out until the 1st of November, and then come in, and do you pay them then or during the summer?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The House has already voted one-sixth of the year's estimates. Out of that we have been able to arrange for the advances for the purchase of supplies, &c., always made to enable the surveyors to take the field. We now require a further sum to pay the expenses during the summer, and the wages. Mi\ OLIVER. In the province of Manitoba the resurveys made by our government are not recognized by the Manitoba government. This has practically tied up our efforts to resurvey lands in Manitoba. We may be able to come to some arrangement with the provincial government which Vill enable us to go forward with these surveys, but are tied up at present.
Mr. -STAPLES. Has there been any correspondence with the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any amount of it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not personal knowledge of the instance mentioned, and cannot give information at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: How much to the 1st of September last?

I thinlr the minister will find five-twelfths sufficient for the actual cash required, and when we come back no doubt the House will provide the balance.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not wi-sh to delay the House if my hon. friends opposite are not willing to pass the item.
Suppose we take two-thirds?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We do not require the whole amount, but more than five-twelfths.
What proportion is required for -contract survey?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Is it not the case that these amounts are largely paid after the surveyor returns in November?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, we do not require the whole of the -money, and probably two-thirds would answer, but we have not made the calculations to enable us to make that division.

There would be no difficulty in the contract surveys getting on

with five-twelfths before the 1st of September.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am very sorry, but I have to say to the committee that five-twelfths will not be sufficient to meet the requirements of the service up to the time that that vote will expire. I say that on my fullest responsibility.

Will the minister also say thart. it is customary to pay five-twelfths before the time mentioned? While I admit that five-twelfths may be earned by that date, is it customary to pay the money before the fall?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have to pay bills as they are presented, and when money is earned it is necessary to provide for the payment. We might possibly get out of paying it, or not be called upon to pay it." On the other hand our surveyors get into jail sometimes because they are not in funds to pay, and we do not want to put them in that position.
There are several sub-items in vote 272 for which I ask consideration. This is the vote for Dominion lands and parks.
One sub-item is:
Contingencies, advertising, &c., $240,000.
This is to pay current expenses, such as the work of the homestead inspector, advertising, printing, and various other matters. The position is the same in regard to this and other items. We do not require the whole amount to carry us through the summer season, but we do require more than five-twelfths.
Is it. field work?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the homestead inspectors, the forest rangers, the fire rangers, and other parties in the field.
Are you asking for the whole amount?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: There was an arrangement made to vote five-twelfths of Supply, and if you are going on making exceptions in this way you will nullify the arrangement.
Has the minister sufficient to put him through until September 1?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, five-twelfths will not carry us until September 1.
How long will it carry you?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Probably until the end of July.
We are to be back here on July 18.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under this vote for Dominion lands and parks, there are the following items to which the same remarks would apply as to the item I have just mentioned. If the committee will vote two-thirds of these amounts we shall be very glad to make the change.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It might be in some items, but not in all. The items to which I refer are:
Dominion. Lands (Surveys, $965,000.
Dominion Lands Contingencies, $240,000. Protection of timber, $255,000.
Irrigation surveys, $68,500.
(St. Mary and Milk rivers, $13,000.
National parks, $201,600.
Water investigations, $20,000.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax), Is that all the minister wants?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All in that item. There are also two items relating to the Yukon, the grant to the Yukon council, and to the roads in the Yukon.
Why do you want these?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Summer is the only time when work can be done on the roads in the Yukon. We are anxious at any rate to have the whole of the road vote.
Why do you want the vote for the council? *

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That involves the general expenditure of the Yukon. However, if the committee will not agree to that I shall be glad to get the road vote, and drop the grant to the Yukon council, except that we get five-twelfths of it.
And you want two-thirds of these amounts?

No, two-thirds of the items referred to under Dominion lands and parks, but I would like the whole of the road vote to the Yukon, because the exnenditure, to be of any use, must be made early in the summer. Then there are two further items in the supplement-aries:
Water investigations, $55,000.
Seed grain advances, $60,000.
The water investigation is to go thoroughly into the question of water in the railway belt of British Columbia in view of the legislation which we have now before

the House, and which we hope to have passed, authorizing the Department of the Interior to deal with that question.
How much do you want?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are asking for $55,000 in the supplementaries.
What proportion?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As the legislation has not passed, perhaps if we took five-twelfths it would answer our purpose. Seed grain, $60,000; that money is already spent, the seed grain is in the ground, and we would like to get the whole of the money. We would like to get two-thirds of the vote for Dominion lands, the whole of the Yukon roads, $50,000. We drop the grants to the Yukon council and surveys in British Columbia.

We are now voting one-half which, with one-sixth already voted, makes two-thirds.
Geological Survey Branch-lor explorations and surveys in Canada, including ethnological archeological and paleontological investigations; and to pay wages of explorers, draughtsmen and others, $142,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is to pay the salaries, expenses and outfitting of the geological parties in the field. Some of them are in the field now, and the rest are going out. We want the whole item if possible. We might be able to do with two-thirds. The expenditures are entirely during the summer. The expenditures are being made now; many of these parties are out in British Columbia, and one or two in the Yukon. Excepting the head of each party, who is an officer of the Geological Survey, all the rest of the men are hired, and have to be paid their monthly wages. We will probably require the whole amount. It would be very desirable if the House would vote the whole sum.
That was not in the list but it was mentioned las't evening.
Harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $40,000.
Kincardine-repairs to piers, $1,500.
Lake Nipissing-improvement of navigable channel in west arm leading through Shanty lake to Monetville, $3,500.
L'Orignal-repairs to wharf and freight shed, $1,000.
McGregor's creek-to pay W. F. Smith, $2,500; O'Keefe and Drew, $320, and the executors of the Poile estate, $1,500, in full and final settlement of all claims for losses sustained owing to damages caused to their properties in the city of Chatham by dredging performed in the creek by a government dredge, $4,320.
Montreal river-removal of boulders in Flat rapids, $3,000.
Pembroke-repairs to wharf and approach, $3,500.

Port Hope-repairs to piers-to construct new superstructure on counterfort on west side of harbour and effect general repairs, $5,000.

Rainy river-improvements at mouth, $60,000.

River Sydenham-second outlet from Chenal Ecarte to Mitchell's bay-protection of banks at Martin island with pile work, $1,000.
Saugeen river-repairs to north and south piers, $1,000.
Sheguiandah-Manitoulin island-repairs to wharf to make good damage by ice shoves, $4,000.
Southampton-harbour improvements, $3,000.
South Nation river-improvement of waterway, $4,000.
Thornbury-repairs to wharf, $1,000.
If any hon. gentleman would state any objection to any item to which there is objection, I would be quite willing to drop it.

I think a chance should be given to the members to make inquiries and ask questions. If we grant one-half now, as we do to the Minister of the Interior, that would give the minister two-thirds altogether. That ought to be sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: All right.
They are all objectionable. We have no objection to giving the hon. gentleman the proportion arranged for, but we can go no further.
Will you give a few of these in addition to what (has been done?

No, I do not think so. Ttie hon. gentleman will not need this money until the end of July when we will be back here. There is no reason for giving more than that called for by the arrangement made between the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition.

I w*ill not discuss the matter. Of course, if it is understood that hon. gentlemen are not willing to allow these items for repairs and work to be done by the day, the responsibility will

not be upon me. In Manitoba there is one item of $8,000 for general repairs and improvements. Repairs are needed in many places, the men have to be employed 'by the day, and I am -sure the public interest will suffer if that work is not done. Is there any objection to that?

There will not be many men employed on day work until after the 18th of July. There will be the five-twelfths of the estimates available which will provide more than is required.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. I understand that is objected to?
Yes, as far as I am concerned.

Very well. Now in Saskatchewan and Alberta there are four items that I urgently ask for. There is the item of:
Harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $20,000.
These are in remote districts where it is necessary to send men to work by the day, and it will he extremely inconvenient if these men have to be recalled.
Where are the works?
They are on the Saskatchewan and Peace rivers and Great Slave lake.

What is the nature of the work?
I am sure that there will be no objection to giving him whatever he wants if *he makes out a good case. But, an arrangement has been entered into between the two leaders.

I did not asume that ,to be the case because when we come back on the 18th July we have special business to take up, but if the leader of the opposition will make that statement, or if my hon. friend speaks with the authority of the other side, Ihen it will be different. I was assuming that when we come back we will not get into supply again perhaps until the autumn.

That is the minister's own look-out. I think that the position that we now take is absolutely reasonable under the circumstances, and we should not be expected to make pledges from one to the other. An arrangement was made and we propose to abide by it.

Then I am to understand that in respect of all the itetas for harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, the maritime provinces generally, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, every item is objected to?

You have the five-twelfths?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. Except what has been allowed.
Removing boulders, improving rapids, doing bridge work and making general improvements to assist navigation in the interest of the traders and settlers.
Do I understand that five-twelfths of these estimates have been arranged for?
Yes.
Then, of that item in Manitoba amounting to $8,000 you have authority to spend five-twelfths?
Yes.
Is not that sufficient until we come back?

No, and I will tell my hon. friend why. The year will not expire until the 31st March next, and while this is supposed to be for the year, this is a class of work that has to be done during the open season. The season closes about the middle of October and therefore the five-twelfths will not enable us to" continue the work beyond midsunimer.
We will be back here on the 18th July, and if the minister will come down with anything that is special

If is not ex-ictly that, Mr. Chairman, if the minister ivill allow me to correct him. We are perfectly willing to take any one of these items and consider it whenever there is :ime and if there is time now. But when the minister asks us to take 449 items and pass them without discussion it is rather a remarkable order particularly in view of the understanding we have had. Among the items which he has presented to us as impressed with urgency I find a great many where the whole amount now asked is a revote, the money having been voted last year, and not a dollar expended You could hardly regard a case of that kind as a very urgent one. I observe a great many items of that kind.
There are some.

A great many. For instance:
West Advocate-breakwater, $10,000.

What province is that
dr. BORDEN (Halifax). In Nova Scotia.
?oulamond wharf-renewals and repairs to perstrueture, $1,600.
iitchfield-extension of breakwater, $4,000.

Liscomb harbour-wharf, $3,000.
Leonard's cove-breakwater, $1,500.
East Bay-wharf, $4,000.
Creignish-construction of landing pier, $2,500.
Central Economy-to renew stem of wharf,

So that the items of urgency do not seem to have been very carefully selected. I told my hon. friend, as he will remember, that I would do what I could to have a limited number of these items, really of a rush character, passed in full, but a wholesale order of 450 items embracing items of the character to which I have just alluded is a very different thing indeed.

Well, suppose we come down to an item in regard to wihidh that objection would not apply. It is not a revote. I refer to item 158 for dredging, vessel repairs and new plant. Hon. gentlemen know that the dre'dging season is the summer season, and the officials of my department inform me that five-twelfths will not carry us along until the close of the summer season. I would, therefore, ask that that item be voted in full.
The whole of it?
The hon. gentleman will find that he has more than plenty to pay what will be required to pay before the 18th July.

No, the difficulty is that we will have to stop the work -before the end of the dredging season. It seems to me that with respect to a great deal of necessary work, I shall have to refuse to give orders to go ahead at all, because the time will come early in the summer when there will be a lot of people clamouring for their pay, and I am not going to be in a position of not being able to pay them. It is very necessary, and the request is not unreasonable.

The minister is making an effort to get political -capital out of this and to try and make the people believe that we are responsible for stopping the work by not voting the money. He has had lots of time to have his estimates passed had he been serious about them. We have been discussing things in this House that were not important at all; we spent two days on a Railway Act which could very well have gone over until after the adjournment, and this morning we were two hours discussing a Grain ~Act which the government must have known could not possibly have been rushed through the House in the very last hours. We do not object to these votes but we want an opportunity to discuss them and to understand them. The minister brings down here three or four hundred items without '

drawing a distinction between those which are urgent and those which are not, and he asks us to swallow them without knowing anything about them. Well, we object to that, and we think the people of the country will say we are right in objecting.

For six or seven weeks early in the session my estimates were discussed day after day, and it was only on the special request of some hon. gentlemen opposite that we deferred the discussion on them and took up the estimates of some other departments. I have no intention of making political capital out of this; I may say there are a number of large items on page 56 which I thought were necessary, but the deputy minister and the assistant deputy minister of the department were requested by me to cut down as closely as possible the items asked for, and to report what in their judgment it was absolutely essential in the public interest should be passed. The list of items which I handed the opposition was made out by the officials without any special instructions from me.

If there is urgency for these items the departmental officers knew it a month ago, and the minister could have arranged with his colleagues to give the discussion of them precedence, but he failed to do that. There is no urgency about it at all.
This very item before us amounts to $2,000,000, and in it is included a revote for dredging in Saskatchewan and Alberta which was not expended last year and was not then considered urgent.
That is for new dredging plant. I put it off until the present year, but the plant is necessary now.
May I ask if this item includes anything for dredging at Port Credit this summer?
I cannot say as to the details of that.
Does not the minister think it is urgent?

I am not sure whether that is on the program for this season or not, but we did some dredging there last year. We are dredging at Oakville in the adjoining constituency and propose working also at Bronte in Halton county. That work is only going to cost $1,400, but if we get at it right away it will be an enormous advantage to the people of the locality. I will not put people to work and not lie able to pay them.

The minister has shown conclusively that he is not in earnest in asking for these votes. The leader of the opposition has demonstrated that the minister made out a list of items which he knew could not be accepted, including a number of revotes for work that was deferred from last year, and for which there was no urgency then. Had he made out a 'list of the urgent items he would have found us reasonable in passing them, but he knew we could not accept the list he presented and he simply endeavoured to put up a big bluff. His action is unfair in that respect.

I would like to believe that my hon. friend (Mr. Perley) is reasonable, but if he says I am unreasonable I am unable to believe that he is reasonable. When he suggests that I am trying to put him in a hole, I answer that it would be cruelty to assist him in getting deeper in that direction than he already is. My officers inform me that all these items are equally urgent, but I suppose if I only brought down twenty items gentlemen opposite would tell me I should only have selected six. On reflection hon. gentlemen will see that this item of dredging ought to be_allowed. Dredging work is to-day as important as any work that can be done for the transportation interests of the country. Steamers are getting larger and in many cases harbours have silted in and in some cases there has been a lowering of water, particularly on the Great Lakes. But what is of the greatest importance is that the steamers are getting larger. There is a great deal of dredging work to be done. The inland waters freeze up in November and unless we can get the work done during the summer, we will be greatly handicapped and the public interest will be greatly prejudiced.

As I understand, the work the hon. gentleman has in mind has not been started yet. In that case five-twelfths of the amount will not have been earned by July 15. The hon. gentleman ignores the fact that we gre voting five-twelfths without discussion, he is asking for the other seven-twelfths. There is no possibility of excuse for saying that more than five-twelfths will be required before the end of July. The hon. gentleman takes care to give the opposition no credit for having voted the five-twelfths.

I suppose I may take it for granted that hon. gentlemen are not willing to pass these items now, and, therefore, I shall not move further in them.
Mr, MAGRATH. Are the recommendations of his officers as to the urgency of these expenditures made in writing?
Made in writing.
Has the hon. gentleman the memorandum?
T shall send to my office for it.

The history of the hon. gentleman's conduct hardly bears out the statement which he makes to-day. He says these things are urgent. He got that information from the engineers of his department. I take the list handed to us yesterday, and I find Port Arthur * $650,000 for dredging, and the minister expects that will all be required before we get back and vote any more. Last year when we voted $600,000 he went on and spent nearly $400,000 more without anv vote, and- he could do it as well this year as. last year.
That is not a desirable thing to do.

I admit that, but it shows that the minister is equal to any emergency when he wishes to do a thing that we have not provided for in the regular way. If the dredges were employed every day they could not use up this amount in that time or anything like it. If urgency was the reason why did the minister discredit himself by putting forward an item like that? It tells the whole tale; it is not a desire to get through items where there is absolute urgency, but to get as many items on the programme as possible, and push them through without inquiry or anything else. The minister said some time ago that earlier in the session some members of the opposition desired that he should refrain from bringing forward his items, and should let other departments bring forward theirs. Why did he do it? Because of the crassness of human nature, that he did not seem willing to give any information to us. and only panned the questions put bv hon. members on this side of the House. In our judgment he did not desire to give information and, therefore, he was kept longer than he should have been to get his items through. Had he shown the same desire as is manifested by other ministers to give all the information possible, the House would have been more amiably inclined to let items go through, even although they had not the information; but it was because of the evident desire to give no information on any question asked, and of his attitude which seemed to say: Well they have to vote it sooner or later, and I will not give the information, I will jolly them along from week to week. When he would not give the information he was delayed from day to day. He said that some of us objected, arid asked to have the estimates of some of the other ministers brought on. That was because of the desire to get some I one who would give information, and not

be frittering away the time of the House as the Minister of Public Works^was doing in handling his estimates before the House when the opposition knew Jie was not sincere in his conduct, and was not making a reasonable effort to give the information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member should not attribute insincerity to another hon. member.
Well then, I shall say his burning desire, and his great sincerity.
Nobody pays serious attention to my hon. friend.
The result was the same.

My hon. friend's memory does not serve him- correctly. I was not complaining of any delay in getting my estimates through, I think they went through with very satisfactory progress indeed. I was greatly pleased at the way in which my hon. friends facilitated the progress of my estimates. They asked' that I should take a rest from the very great labour which they thought was being imposed on me working day after day and night after night, but I had nothing but feelings of gratification at the manner in which the hon. gentlemen facilitated the passage of the estimates. I have now the memorandum to which I referred, it is as follows:
Office of the Deputy Minister,
Ottawa, May 13, 1911. Memorandum to the Minister:-
The department is going to be greatly handicapped in its work this year owing to the full amounts of appropriations not being available. As you will realize, it is not possible, under such circumstances, to commence works by day labour. Where work is done that way, the money must be forthcoming to pay wages, and, in addition to that, it would not be good business to employ a foreman and a number of men, buy timber and commence repairing a wharf; get half way through and dismiss the whole lot, and take them on again two or three months later to finish the balance of the work.
As you are aware, one-sixth of the harbour and river appropriations .in the .main estimates have been voted, and possibly before the House adjourns next week, a further portion of one-third will be voted, making one-half >n all; but even so, our position as above outlined would not 'be much improved. Works could only be begun and left half finished, which would not be either economical or businesslike.
However, as hon. gentlemen take the view that it is not in the public interest that provision should be made for going on with these various works to which I have referred', I shall not press the matter any further
Hon. gentlemen have not taken that view. Hon. gentlemen believe that the works can be carried on in

a business like way and successfully carried on with the amount they are willing to vote in most of these cases. An odd work might be picked out here and there where the circumstances were different, but it was because of the desire of the minister to select a great list of items about many of which there could be no urgency, and which could be proceeded with in the regular wav until the House resumes, that we were faced with the dilemma of not knowing what to give or what to withhold. Many of the items mentioned by the leader of the opposition were revotes, some of them have been in for two years in succession, and now it becomes terribly urgent that the money should be voted, although the money has been voted for two or three years without a stroke being done. Yet for three years not a stroke of work has been done. These things indicate to us. that the minister can scarcely be sincere in saying there is special urgency.
Mr. BLA1N. Since the minister has said that the opposition assisted him very materially in putting through his estimates in the earlier part of the session, liow many estimates were put through in his department? There must be a large number.

During the early part of the session, I think all the public buildings through the Dominion were voted in full with the exception of some armouries.
To complete payment incurred in the Norji Atlantic coast fisheries arbitration before the Hague Tribunal-Revote, $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I want to explain the necessity for this revote. About two months ago an item, of which this is in part a revote, was considered by this committee; and after some discussion, the committee voted $100,000 to complete the disbursements in connection with expenses at the Hague. My hon. friend fram East Hamilton (Mr. Barker) took considerable part in the discussion and will no doubt recollect the circumstances. That item was included in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March last, and as a result any unexpended portion lapsed on the 30th April. There remain still some accounts to pay, and as these accounts are overdue, and ought to be settled, I have taken the liberty of asking that this amount be voted now in full.
General protection of highways, $135,000.

This is an item for the subways and protection of level crossings on the Intercolonial railway. The urgency of the case is this, traffic must he continued, and we cannot take any chance of getting a subway partly through and then having to leave it incomplete.
Are these contracts all made?
No, a good deal is done by our own men. This will include twelve level crossings.
If this is done by permanent employees, we pay them by the month or fortnight, and will not have to pay more than five-twelfths by the time we meet again.

Welland ship canal-To complete survey. $50,000.

For the decoration of public buildings throughout Canada in connection with the celebration of the coronation of His Majesty the King, $25,000.

What is the plan for expending this money?

I have conferred with the officials in my department, and it is thought that $25,000 will be sufficient to do a reasonable amount of decorating of public buildings throughout the country. There seems to be, as we have learned from communications sent to us, a desire in many sections of the country to celebrate the coronation of his Majesty. But I have had applications from different places, and I am sure that the people generally expect that we will take some part in the celebration in the way proposed.
Will each small town that has a public building get a portion of this money for the purposes of decoration?

There are three small towns in my locality that have public buildings, and I think they ought to have their share of the money, so that they may make a decent showing on that occasion, if we are to spend any money for that purpose. should not be the municipality. But if it is the opinion of the House that we ought to spend money in that way, I think there ought to be a sufficient allowance so that every town with public buildings might have a chance to get a portion of it for the purpose of decorating such buildings.

On section 1,

The explanations that I gave in moving the resolution the other day are complete as regards the classification, the changes, and the increase. There are many minor details which add to the length of the Bill, but I shall ask the House to take for granted the explanations I gave the other day as to its general scope.

There is no doubt that the post office employees in our larger cities are suffering from a very considerable grievance on account of the difference between their salaries and the salaries of other civil servants, therefore it seems to me that the principle of this Bill cannot be opposed. At the same time we have not carried the Civil Service reform through all the branches of the service as we should have done. When we found that the excellent reform introduced by this government for the inside service worked satisfactorily, we should, without any unnecessary delay, have carried those reforms to the outside service. We did not do so because there is no doubt the government in reforming the inside service cut off from members of this House a patronage with which they were not willing to part, and we have continued for the outside service a system which is universally condemned. This has caused many inconveniences and disadvantages to the public at large, and to the Civil Service itself because the inequalities that existed for years in the outside service have been maintained, and we have found in the outside service new employees gaining government patronage and enjoying large salaries when really old and meritorious employees were less generously treated than these newcomers. That system will continue as long as we do not carry the reform from the inside to the outside service. The Postmaster General some time ago increased the salaries of the letter carriers. Their salaries were increased 40 per cent, and they undoubtedly deserved that increase. I believe that the letter carriers in the larger cities, like Montreal and Toronto, are to-day not sufficiently paid when you consider the work they have to do, the trust that is imposed in them and the expenses which have so greatly increased in our large cities. They have had an increase of 40 per cent, and yet men working alongside of them in the post offices have received no increase. The customs employees were increased some time ago 33J per cent. There is no reason why they should be increase and the post office employees should not be increased. What is the increase which my hon. friend provides for in this Bill? It is an increase of $50 a year except in the case of employees who belong to a class who receive on ap-

pointment $500. Take the case of a man in a large city who has been in the employ of the country for 20, 25, or 30 years, and who receives $1,000. He belongs to a class where the increase will be only $50 a year until he receives $1,200 which will be in four years, an increase of $4 a month. It does not seem to me that that is a fair increase. I have in mind the case of a man who has been 38 years in the public service, and who has belonged to the second class since 1887. He will receive an increase of $50 a year during the next four years in order to reach the maximum of his class. Another one whose case was brought to my attention in Montreal receives $1,000 after 26 years' service. These two men have been in positions of great trust, and have always given perfect satisfaction. Their salaries are, by common admission absolutely inadequate, yet they are to get an increase of $200 extending over four years or $4 a month. That is not a fair increase, it is not at all on the same footing as the increases in other branches of the service unless, as my hon. friend has stated, I do not understand the Act, and that it is intended to take these old employees from the class in which they are and put them in another class, say above the $1,200 maximum, where they will go from $1,200 to $1,600. Even in that case it does not seem to me that the increase given to those men is sufficient unless they skip a class and are put in a class quite above that in which they have been for so many years. These old employees And themselves working alongside men who have been appointed within the last two or three or five years, who receive the same salary, or very nearly the same salary, and some, I believe I can say truthfully, even more. This is not the proper way to ensure a good Civil Service in these large post offices where the bulk of the work devolves upon these very old and experienced employees who really conduct the business of the office. With regard to post office employees in Montreal generally, they do their work excellently, the cases of dereliction of duty and breaches of trust particularly are extremely rare when you consider the large responsibilities upon the employees.
I have no hesitation in saying that if in the city of Montreal, the system which has worked so well in the interior were transferred to the outside, at any rate in the Postal department, we would have a much larger revenue. In London, if you drop a letter into a box at a certain hour, you are sure that at a given hour it will be delivered into any other part of the city, but you cannot depend on anything of the kind in Montreal. This session, letters I (have sent from Ottawa to Montreal have been detained 24 hours. I do 302
not blame the officials because they are heavily worked and not neglectful but the system is bad. In Montreal we cannot rely on letters being promptly delivered there as they are elsewhere. Consequently when you want a letter delivered at a certain hour, you have to use other means than the postal service. Unless my hon. friend will do justice to these older employees by taking them out of their present position and putting them in a superior class, flhe advantages to them from this Bill will be very small. A man at $1,000 a year, who has given a quarter of a century to the service of his country, will stand to get an increase to $1,200 in four years. Of course it will be open to my hon. friend to change, his class, but the time has arrived to carry the reform from the interior to the outside service. The only obstacle in the way is the desire to give a sop of patronage to members of parliament. In the United States they have carried civil service reform very much further tfhan we have. They began with the customs in New York, where the spoils system had produced the worst results. That system is entirely done away with, and the postal service has been considerably improved also. I would invite my hon. friend to carry civil service reform into the postal department throughout the outside service, and in this way considerably increase our postal revenue.

The other night when we discussed the resolution, the minister gave us to understand that the men in the service were perfectly satisfied with the increases. But since the wording of the Bill has been made known, I have received several letters and telegrams from men in the service, indicating that tthey are anything but satisfied. Here is one telegram which I received:
Bill much less favourable than appears. Clerks greatly disappointed.
I had another letter from a clerk who pointed out to me that in a good many cases a large percentage were receiving practically no benefit from the increase. There is no doubt that the object of these resolutions was to increase the salaries of different clerks in the post office and railway mail service; but in the way these increases are proposed, in some cases the clerks have to work five or six years before they begin to derive any benefit. Take a clerk who is now at $900, he will (have to work ten years before he gets to the top of this increase or six years until he gets to the present maximum of $1,200. Then he begins to derive some benefit from what we are given to believe is an increase at present. It is not much of an increase the clerks are getting now. They are al-



ready getting {50 inciease in their salary per year, and have to go on working six years before they participate in the increases given under the new Bill. After thinking this matter over, perhaps the Postmaster General will consider favourably some of these things, and make the increase from {800 instead of from {1,000. That would be some sort of an important increase. It would be something in the way of an immediate increase to the men. There is no doubt that they have the same reason to expect an increase that the men of the inside service hhve. I do not see why there should not be an increase to the outside service as well as to the inside service who happen to be under the Civil Service Act. All are public servants of the Dominion, anti all give good Teturns for the salaries they receive. We should do justice to all public servants. But I suppose I need not deal at greater length with this question. The Postmaster General understands what we need. We desire some real benefit to the employees, and I think that what I have asked is not in any way unreasonable.

I desire to move, in conformity with what I stated a few moments ago, to add to the section the following proviso :
Provided that a new classification of all employees referred to in the foregoing section, whose term of employment in the public service exceed ten years, be effected upon the coming into force of the present Act, so as to ensure to said employees a salary proportioned to the duration of their services as compared with the salaries of officers more recently appointed.
I suppose the minister will have no objection to this. He says this is the principle that will guide him in the application of the law.

I do not think that, at the present stage, I could take it upon my.self to accept the amendment. I told my hon. friend (Mr. Monk), that the Bill as framed is exactly on the classification adopted for the inside service, and no added words of mine, or of my hon. friend could perfect it so far as that is concerned. He stated a moment ago that we should carry out as soon as possible the principle that the employees in the outside service in the larger cities should come under the Civil Service Act. If my hon. friend had been here the other day, and had listened to the long discussion which took place on the Bill he would have learned that that is my policy. We take the first step this year in classifying the clerks and employees in the post offices of the Dominion ag they are classified in the Post Office Department. The next step, and one that I intend to take, but to which parliament as a whole perhaps, is not yet committed, is the bring-Mr. RUSSELL.
ing of the outside officers under the operation of the Civil Service Act. That pledge I have given to the House, and I intend to carry it through. The Bill has been framed very carefully by the officers of the department, and I could not alter the wording of it. All 1 can say is that the older employees in the service will benefit by the Bill. I am told by my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Russell), that the increase is very small. I .heard the ^speech of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), the other night about the bank clerks; and that, and other things lead me to believe that the salaries in the post office will compare with the salaries in our financial institutions, and in other employments. The young man is appointed at {500 and gets a Taise of {100 if he behaves well. He goes up to {800, to {.1,000, to {1,200, to {1,600, and if he is a clever man, and knows how to make his way, if he shows some intelligence and some diligence in his readings he will soon be one of the best employees in the service. Examinations-we call them case examinations.-are required' every six months. This, as I said, is the first step. According to the arrangement, not by the whim or caprice of the minister, but by the reorganization of the post office system, there will be regular case examinations, and the best men in the service can have a chance to assert themselves, and to get increases. Again I say, that as a whole the increases are quite substantial, and will offer an opportunity to every diligent officer in the department. My hon. friend from East Toronto says he has heard many complaints about the increases. Well, my experience is that no man in the service is pleased when he gets {200 of an increase if he expected to get {250 or {300. But there must be a limit, and that limit is a question of policy. The government as a whole say that those employees can be increased to a certain limit, and not beyond. This is a charge upon the public revenues. I told the hon. gentleman the other day that the total increase of the employees of the post office would amount this year to over {51,000. Three years ago, we increased the letter carriers, which meant another charge on the public revenues, I made that increase cheerfully, and I think that the letter carriers as a body, are satisfied. Their salaries will reach {2.75 a day. Of course, there are a few agitators who can never be satisfied, who think they are entitled. to salaries equal to the indemnity of a member of parliament, or the. salary of a minister of the Crown. We cannot satisfy these agitators. The less work they do the more highly they think they are entitled to be paid. But, as I have said, the great majority of these men are satisfied. Of course, if they are encouraged by gentlemen who pat them on the shoulder and

say: Why do you not have some more? You are getting $2.75, but you ought to get $3. Demand it; the minister will give it to you. If they are talked to in that way dissatisfaction may increase. Of course, I am only administering a trust for the people of Canada, but I think from the expressions of opinion I have heard, the people are satisfied. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), spoke of young men in banks twenty and twenty-five years of age receiving $400 a year.
Why, Sir, in the Post Office Department they receive $500 on appointment, and an annual increase of $100 until they reach the maximum of their class. Then if they are diligent, if they are intelligent, if they show some .ability, they are taken into a higher class. But the man who simply performs his work in an easy way, who is always looking at the clock to leave the office, that man will not get beyond the maximum of his class. Now as regards the pull, or such influences as are mentioned by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), let me tell him this: During the last five years that I have been Postmaster General I have made very few appointments to positions carrying large salaries. I have in mind two or three officers who have been appointed to the higher positions. Let me mention the post office inspector at Ottawa, Mr. Bolduc, a brother of Senator Bolduc, belonging to a Conservative family, and a Conservative himself. He had served for twenty years in the Quebec district. I did not consider his political leanings, I only knew that he was the best man in the service in the province of Quebec, and I gave him that lift. I have in mind also another post office inspector whom I appointed the other day in Quebec to succeed Mr. Caouette. He had served the public for many years in the post office, and I was reminded by some of my friends that I should have taken a Liberal. But that gentleman is a man of ability, he has had a large experience, and that is the keystone of the whole service. Then I selected Mr. Green, of Quebec, a gentleman whose politics I do not know, but everybody admits that he was by far the best man', and I believe he was aiso an Irishman. In the higher positions of the service, the best men always reach the top.

I would like to ask the
minister a question. Under present conditions and regulations, is the department getting satisfactory men in the railway mail service? Have they any difficulty in maintaining the service with satisfactory men?

The only difficulty I find in getting men for the railway mail service is to find those who are able to 302J
pass the qualifying examinations. Otherwise, we get hundreds of men who are ready to serve as railway mail clerks, but they are not able to pass the qualifying examination. We are obliged to take them on as labourers, in twenty-five cases, out of forty, and give them a chance to learn their runs, and after a while they are able to pass the examination. But it is when the time comes to appoint railway mail clerks who can pass an examination without coming into the service first as labourers that we find difficulty. Later on they pass the examination and are appointed regularly. My hon. friend may be sure that we have hundreds and thousands of applications for the position, and the minister and the members are pestered through 'the applications we receive.

Is there any way in which you make the position attractive enough to get men who could qualify? When you get men who are able to qualify at the start, would you necessarily send for them from among the labourers you take in and train?

When the Postmaster General institutes a comparison between a post office employee and a bank employee he cannot afford to forget, the fact that a bank offers rewards for merit, and a preferment which the Post Office Department does not offer.

A man can get to the top in the Post Office Department if he possesses the necessary energy and industry. The best men in the service are those who fought their way up from the bottom, who showed pluck and industry.

I quite agree. But I say that even if a post office employee does reach the top, the reward he gets on reaching the top is nothing in comparison with the reward a bank employee receives who reaches the top in his calling.
What is the reward of the bank employee? The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) told us the other night.

My hon. friend from Grey was referring to the ordinary employee of a bank. But human nature is so constituted that a man is willing to take a very small salary for his labour if the goal of his ambition offers a very high one, and if the reward when he reaches that goal is a great one. I want to point out to the minister that he cannot afford to overlook that fact, and that since he is not offering that great reward to the man who attains the goal of his ambition in the Post Office Department, it is the duty of a minister, and of the country to pay liberally the men for the work they perform in the service.

Mr. GRAHAM moved that the House go into Committee of the Whole to consider the following resolutions:
Whereas, by chapter 25, of the Statutes of 1910, it was provided that the Minister of Railways and Canals might, subject to the terms and couditions therein contained, lease lines of railway connecting with the government railways and operate them as a part of the government railways, but no leases have been made under the said Act: And, whereas, it is deemed advisable to make the provisions hereinafter contained for the leasing of the undermentioned line of railway. Therefore, it is resolved that it is expedient that the Minister of Railways and Canals be authorized, with the approval of the Governor in Council, to lease for a term not exceeding 99 years the following line of railway, namely:-The Bale railway, prc-perty of the Acadia Coal Company, Limited, extending from New Glasgow to Thorburn, iu the province of Nova Scotia, a distance of about six miles, upon terms and conditions to be approved of by the Government Railways Managing Board; provided, however, that the consideration by way of ren tal for such line of railway shall he an annual rental of one dollar and the carriage of the traffic of the company, its successors and assigns, upon the line of railway to be leased and upon the government railways, and between points to be designated and at rates not in excess of maximum fixed rates for such carriage between such points, such fixed rates to he subject to a provision for revision of such rates at the end of each period of 10 years during the continuance of the lease.
Such railway so leased shall become and be operated as a part of the government railways.
He said: Of course I do not hope to get these resolutions through to-night; but as we have a few moments to wait, I think it would be the part of wisdom for me to say a few words about these branch lines, so that hon. gentlemen can find them on ' Hansard,' and have an opportunity of thinking the subject over during the recess, and he able more intelligently to take it up again when the House reassembles. The great majority of the lines that might be available under lease to the Intercolonial are placed under two resolutions. The first "one referred to as the Vale railway, is a short road a little over five miles long, running out of New Glasgow, and owned by the Acadia Coal Company.
It really does its own traffic, and it is very desirable from the standpoint of the Intercolonial that, if reasonable arrangements can be made, that road should come under government control, and be leased as part of the government railways. The Acadia Coal Company owns the railway, and owns the 'Coal mines, and really does its own business, and little else. Just beyond the property of the Acadia coal mines there are other coal areas that might, so it has been represented to me, be well developed. But as one coal mine or coal company owns the railway, it does not at all encourage the development of the other coal areas by assisting them to carry their traffic. It has been represented to the department, and to the board of management that this road could he secured, not by the payment of any cash, but merely by an arrangement with them for a term of years as to the freight rates on their coal. Of course the Intercolonial would get all the traffic, as it does now, but it would be in the interest of the railway as well, to acquire that line. The Teason it is put in a separate resolution is, as I have said, that it can be acquired without the usual terms of lease, by an arrangement as to freight rates, and without the payment of any cash.
The other lines can hardly be said to be paying in themselves, apart from the government railway system, if we take them as single entities. The majority of them have a surplus of receipts- over expenses now, hut if we were to lease them, and pay interest on a certain amount, probably there would not be any surplus, probably there would be a deficit, treating them as mere entities, each line by itself. But this much must be borne in mind, I say it on behalf of the state owned railway, that it will not be long until other railway lines must have certain rights over the Intercolonial, or they will have to build a line from St. John to Halifax themselves. The Grand Trunk Pacific has running rights, under its contract, over the Intercolonial from Moncton to St. John, and from St. John to Halifax. Merely looking at these lines as entities in themselves, as not paying much, or not paying at all, should some other line secure any of these branches that now feed the Intercolonial, it would be a very serious thing for the state owneld railway.	That is one
side of it. The other side is the interest of the people.	Now, leaving
out of the question what detriment it would be to the state owned railway, and the decrease in the value of our property if these branch lines with their traffic were to be diverted to some other private owned road, there is another aspect.' Some of these roads governments have aided, and their operation is unsatisfactory. I will give an extreme case, the Salisbury and

Albert road has ceased operation over a certain portion of it, the department has been advised. The people who for years have had railway facilities given them by this line, are at the present moment without any railway facilities. The government of Canada has aided that line, although it has I think a provincial charter. I presume the provincial government has also aided it, and the county itself gave aid. But notwithstanding all that, the people along that line of railway are now deprived of all railway facilities. I am bold enough to take the ground that it is the duty of some government to afford facilities to those people that formerly had them, even if it should cost some money. That is one class of line. The other class will come into the category I mentioned a few moments ago. It will be an immense detriment to the Intercolonial if they pass into other hands. I am not going into details at all, but I want the members of this House during recess to think over the situation of those lines, and ask themselves whether it is not advisable to give the Department of Railways power, under the terms outlined in the resolutions, which are very much restricted, to secure these lines, or a portion of them at least, for the reasons I have stated. On the other hand, where people are likely to be deprived, and have been deprived in some instances, of the railway transportation they have enjoyed for years, is it not our duty to do something in that respect? I submit the resolutions for the consideration of the House during the recess, so that when they come back they will be able, I hope, to support the measure.

I would like to ask the minister what position those lines will be in whose bonds are guaranteed by the provincial government, and I think where the provincial government holds a mortgage on the railway? What position would that railway hold after it was leased by this government?

That is a question to be investigated by a judge of the Exchequer Court. _ My hon. friend will see in this resolution that the present condition of a line of that kind, its indebtedness, -where it is, and what the remuneration ought to be, will be investigated by a judge of the Exchequer Court. It strikes me that in a case of that kind probably some arrangement might be made, but at least on most of the _ lines I imagine interest is not being paid to any one on the bonds.

Mr. Speaker, I would not for a moment, at this stage, attempt to discuss the resolutions, but I have taken considerable interest in this matter. Indeed, I have had the honour of first bringing to the notice of parliament and the government the whole question of the absorption of the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway, and I think it is due to myself that I should say some few words in respect to the resolutions. If I were to evince a little exaltation with regard to the government having met my views, at least measurably, perhaps, I would be pardoned. However, my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), has thrown out some ideas which he wishes hon. members to consider during the adjournment. There are a_ few things that I would like him consider during the adjournment, and one is this, that _ in an undertaking of this character it is well-and I suppose we all recognize it-that two interests should be considered; first, the interests of the Intercolonial railway, second, the interests of the communities served by these several branch lines, and you might say, third, the interests of the whole country. But, as I understand it, the Intercolonial railway interests are representative of the interests of the whole of Canada. Now, I regret that there are one or two omissions with respect to railways in the province of Nova Scotia. I refer to the coal railways in the county of Cumberland. There is an omission of the power of expropriation with respect to some of these roads, or in respect to all of them. In a word, I would like to make my meaning clear in this regard. I hold that if there were power of expropriation given the government of Canada to take over some of these roads it would only be protecting the interests of the Intercolonial railway, and therefore, the interests of Canada, and it would enable them to secure lines of rail-

way which they might not be able to secure under the provisions of these resolutions. For instance, the coal railways in the county of Cumberland are so situated. One is the Maritime Coal and Railway Company, and the other is the Cumberland Coal and Railway Company. The first named is known as the Joggins road, or coal mine. The Maritime Coal and Railway Company have a line running from Maccan to Joggins mine a distance of 12 miles, and it is known as the Joggins railway. There are five distinct coal mines on that line of railway, tout the Josrgins mine so called is owned by the railway company. The other mines are owned by separate corporations. One is the Strath-cona mine, another is the Jubilee mine, another the Minudie mine, another the Fundy mine, and I think that there is still another tract or area known as the Boston area. These five companies, other than the coal and railway company, are placed at a very great disadvantage by reason of the fact that the railway company operate a coal mine on that same line of railway to the detriment of the other mines, and the result is a depreciation in the value of the coal mined by these separate corporations. It seems to me that in the interest of the Intercolonial railway the government should be in a position to secure that line whether the coal and railway company desire it or not. The Tight of eminent domain should apply and the powers of expropriation should be given, in the interests of the whole country, and in the interests of those several mines that are lying along the same route. The same condition applies to the Cumberland Coal and Railway Company which operates in connection with the Springhill mine. This js a railway running from Springhill Junction on the Intercolonial railway to tide-water at Parrsboro, in the county of Cumberland. That company operate lines, they own the railway, and there are several coal mining areas which are absolutely precluded from being developed by reason of the conditions resulting from the ownership of that railway. If the government had the power of expropriation they could secure these lines. The coal and railway companies as owners are not interested in parting with thesp roads. They make large dividends out of the operation of the railways, and while provision is made with respect to some of these railways there are many of them which will not take advantage of the opportunity of leasing or even selling their roads to the government of Canada in order that they might become a portion of the Intercolonial railway system. Then, theTe is the New Brunswick and Prince Edwrard Island Tail-wav, which, to my mind, commands the traffic of Prince Edward Island and is the key to the situation with respect to that
traffic. The Minister of Railways has said very clearly and distinctly that to the extent to which any of these branch lines are secured by any great private railway corporation the valuable asset of the government in the Intercolonial railway is thereby depreciated. We must look forward to the fact that as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have running rights over the Intercolonial railway from Moncton to Halifax, and from Moncton to St. John, so must the Canadian Pacific Railway Company secure those rights. So must the Canadian Northern in time secure those same running rights, and if one of these railways in the meantime were to step in and secure this New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway, secure the Albert railway, and secure some others of these branch lines the main trunk line would be depreciated in value. If the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have it in mind to secure any portion of the Intercolonial railway, either by purchase or by lease, or if the Canadian Northern have any such idea in their minds, naturally, as a business proposition, they would secure some of its main feeders, and securing them they would depreciate the value of the government asset, the value of the Intercolonial railway, and, therefore, they could derive a better bargain.
They would be in a position to say to the government of Canada:	We have control
of the branches which supply traffic, and to that extent the Intercolonial railway would be depreciated in value, and that would be a very easy way for any railway corporation to secure for practically a song the Intercolonial for their own use and benefit. Therefore, as a matter of protection the government should take power of expropriation. There are measures before parliament to-day to build new branches ' for the Intercolonial railway, and power of expropriation is given with respect to the right of way, and in order to protect the interests of the people, and of the Intercolonial railway the same principle should apply with respect to these branch lines. I already have evidence that one of these railways was secured by private individuals within the last six weeks for speculative purposes; in my judgment, for the mere purpose of holding it as against the Intercolonial railway, and playing off the Canadian Pacific railway, or the Canadian Northern railway as against the Intercolonial railway. Having secured this road they would have the Intercolonial railway and the government at a disadvantage in the event of any attempt on their part either with respect to securing running rights or leasehold interest on any particular portion of the Intercolonial railway. I ask the Min-

ister of Railways to consider during the adjournment, if, in self-protection, it would not be advisable to incorporate in this resolution a clause to secure powers of expropriation. If there were a clause giving the minister power to expropriate and exercise the right of eminent domain, we would be in a better position to deal with the owners of these several branch lines. I strongly urge upon him the advisability of carrying out this idea. It seems to me that the minister should by all means add to the list of railways to be secured the railway known as the Maritime Coal and Railway Company's road, and also the Cumberland Coal and Railway Company's road, the one 12 miles long and the other 30 miles long, speaking from memory. I know the value of many of these roads. The possibilities of the road formerly known as the Baie des Chaleurs railway are immense. The great fishing and lumber resources of Bonaven-ture and Gaspe counties cannot fail to make that railway in years to come one of the best paying roads the government could secure. Then the International road running from Campbellton to the St. John river protects the Intercolonial railway in its American traffic, it being a short line by which to convey to the New England market the stone and fish and great natural resources of that territory. Then, the Cara-quet road running from Bathurst to Shipe-gan and Tracadie traverses a country second to none in Canada as it runs through the county of Gloucester rich in mineral, lumbering, fishing and agricultural resources. That railway would add very materially to the value of the Intercolonial railway. Then there are the Kent Northern, and the Moncton and Buctouche railway in the county of Kent which are valuable pieces of line. Then the Albert railway traverses a district, the richest in mineral resources in eastern Canada. The great shale district, the rich natural gas and oil district of the county of Albert, and the great plaster industry predict for the future of that road as well as for the Salisbury and Harvey line great prosperity. The Intercolonial railway should secure that, and it should not be left to the whim of owners or speculators as to whether the people of Canada should or should not have these railways. It is a business proposition in the interests of the property of the people of Canada, and it should be so managed that no band of speculators, and no little corporation, or no aggregation of corporations should be allowed to hold up the people of Canada in securing leasehold rights in these railways. From a business standpoint there should be the right of expropriation, in justice to the Intercolonial railway, and to the communities which are served by these branch lines.
